mn: Those who have entirely renounced (all things and all desire) have obtained (absorption into God); all others wander in confusion, entangled in the net of (many) births

tr: When that which clings falls off, severed is being's tie; All else will then be seen as instability
mn: At the moment in which desire has been abandoned, (other) births will be cut off; when that has not been done, instability will be seen

tr: Cling thou to that which He, to Whom nought clings, hath bid thee cling, Cling to that bond, to get thee free from every clinging thing
mn: Desire the desire of Him who is without desire; in order to renounce desire, desire that desire

tr: Of things devoid of truth as real things men deem;-Cause of degraded birth the fond delusive dream
mn: Inglorious births are produced by the confusion (of mind) which considers those things to be real which are not real

tr: Darkness departs, and rapture springs to men who see, The mystic vision pure, from all delusion free
mn: A clear, undimmed vision of things will deliver its possessors from the darkness of future births, and confer the felicity (of heaven)

tr: When doubts disperse, and mists of error rollAway, nearer is heav'n than earth to sage's soul
mn: Heaven is nearer than earth to those men of purified minds who are freed from from doubt

tr: Five-fold perception gained, what benefits accrueTo them whose spirits lack perception of the true
mn: Even those who have all the knowledge which can be attained by the five senses, will derive no benefit from it, if they are without a knowledge of the true nature of things

tr: Whatever thing, of whatsoever kind it be,'Tis wisdom's part in each the very thing to see
mn: (True) knowledge is the perception concerning every thing of whatever kind, that that thing is the true thing

tr: Who learn, and here the knowledge of the true obtain, Shall find the path that hither cometh not again
mn: They, who in this birth have learned to know the True Being, enter the road which returns not into this world

tr: The mind that knows with certitude what is, and ponders well, Its thoughts on birth again to other life need not to dwell
mn: Let it not be thought that there is another birth for him whose mind having thoroughly considered (all it has been taught) has known the True Being

tr: When folly, cause of births, departs; and soul can viewThe truth of things, man's dignity- 'tis wisdom true
mn: True knowledge consists in the removal of ignorance; which is (the cause of) births, and the perception of the True Being who is (the bestower of) heaven

tr: The true 'support' who knows- rejects 'supports' he sought before-Sorrow that clings all destroys, shall cling to him no more
mn: He who so lives as to know Him who is the support of all things and abandon all desire, will be freed from the evils which would otherwise cleave to him and destroy (his efforts after absorption)

tr: When lust and wrath and error's triple tyranny is o'er, Their very names for aye extinct, then pain shall be no more
mn: If the very names of these three things, desire, anger, and confusion of mind, be destroyed, then will also perish evils (which flow from them)

tr: The wise declare, through all the days, to every living thingThat ceaseless round of birth from seed of strong desire doth spring
mn: (The wise) say that the seed, which produces unceasing births, at all times, to all creatures, is desire

tr: If desire you feel, freedom from changing birth require!'I' will come, if you desire to 'scape, set free from all desire
mn: If anything be desired, freedom from births should be desired; that (freedom from births) will be attained by desiring to be without desire

tr: No glorious wealth is here like freedom from desire; To bliss like this not even there can soul aspire
mn: There is in this world no excellence equal to freedom from desire; and even in that world, there is nothing like it

tr: Desire's decease as purity men know; That, too, from yearning search for truth will grow
mn: Purity (of mind) consists in freedom from desire; and that (freedom from desire) is the fruit of the love of truth

tr: Men freed from bonds of strong desire are free; None other share such perfect liberty
mn: They are said to be free (from future birth) who are freed from desire; all others (who, whatever else they may be free from, are not freed from desire) are not thus free

tr: Desire each soul beguiles; True virtue dreads its wiles
mn: It is the chief duty of (an ascetic) to watch against desire with (jealous) fear; for it has power to deceive (and destroy) him

tr: Who thoroughly rids his life of passion-prompted deed, Deeds of unfailing worth shall do, which, as he plans, succeed
mn: If a man thoroughly cut off all desire, the deeds, which confer immortality, will come to him, in the path in which he seeks them

tr: Affliction is not known where no desires abide; Where these are, endless rises sorrow's tide
mn: There is no sorrow to those who are without desire; but where that is, (sorrow) will incessantly come, more and more

tr: When dies away desire, that woe of woesEv'n here the soul unceasing rapture knows
mn: Even while in this body, joy will never depart (from the mind, in which) desire, that sorrow of sorrows, has been destroyed

tr: Drive from thy soul desire insatiate; Straight'way is gained the moveless blissful state
mn: The removal of desire, whose nature it is never to be satisfied, will immediately confer a nature that can never be changed

tr: Wealth-giving fate power of unflinching effort brings; From fate that takes away idle remissness springs
mn: Perseverance comes from a prosperous fate, and idleness from an adverse fate

tr: The fate that loss ordains makes wise men's wisdom foolishness; The fate that gain bestows with ampler powers will wisdom bless
mn: An adverse fate produces folly, and a prosperous fate produces enlarged knowledge

tr: In subtle learning manifold though versed man be,'The wisdom, truly his, will gain supremacy
mn: Although (a man) may study the most polished treatises, the knowledge which fate has decreed to him will still prevail

tr: Two fold the fashion of the world: some live in fortune's light; While other some have souls in wisdom's radiance bright
mn: There are (through fate) two different natures in the world, hence the difference (observable in men) in (their acquisition of) wealth, and in their attainment of knowledge

tr: All things that good appear will oft have ill success; All evil things prove good for gain of happiness
mn: In the acquisition of property, every thing favourable becomes unfavourable, and (on the other hand) everything unfavourable becomes favourable, (through the power of fate)

tr: Things not your own will yield no good, howe'er you guard with pain; Your own, howe'er you scatter them abroad, will yours remain
mn: Whatever is not conferred by fate cannot be preserved although it be guarded with most painful care; and that, which fate has made his, cannot be lost, although one should even take it and throw it away

tr: Save as the 'sharer' shares to each in due degree, To those who millions store enjoyment scarce can be
mn: Even those who gather together millions will only enjoy them, as it has been determined by the disposer (of all things)

tr: The destitute with ascetics merit share, If fate to visit with predestined ills would spare
mn: The destitute will renounce desire (and become ascetics), if (fate) do not make them suffer the hindrances to which they are liable, and they pass away

tr: When good things come, men view them all as gain; When evils come, why then should they complain
mn: How is it that those, who are pleased with good fortune, trouble themselves when evil comes, (since both are equally the decree of fate) ?

tr: What powers so great as those of Destiny? Man's skillSome other thing contrives; but fate's beforehand still
mn: What is stronger than fate ? If we think of an expedient (to avert it), it will itself be with us before (the thought)

tr: An army, people, wealth, a minister, friends, fort: six things-Who owns them all, a lion lives amid the kings
mn: He who possesses these six things, an army, a people, wealth, ministers, friends and a fortress, is a lion among kings

tr: Courage, a liberal hand, wisdom, and energy: these fourAre qualities a king adorn for evermore
mn: Never to fail in these four things, fearlessness, liberality, wisdom, and energy, is the kingly character

tr: A sleepless promptitude, knowledge, decision strong:These three for aye to rulers of the land belong
mn: These three things, viz, vigilance, learning, and bravery, should never be wanting in the ruler of a country

tr: Kingship, in virtue failing not, all vice restrains, In courage failing not, it honour's grace maintains
mn: He is a king who, with manly modesty, swerves not from virtue, and refrains from vice

tr: A king is he who treasure gains, stores up, defends, And duly for his kingdom's weal expends
mn: He is a king who is able to acquire (wealth), to lay it up, to guard, and to distribute it

tr: Where king is easy of access, where no harsh word repels, That land's high praises every subject swells
mn: The whole world will exalt the country of the king who is easy of access, and who is free from harsh language

tr: With pleasant speech, who gives and guards with powerful liberal hand, He sees the world obedient all to his command
mn: The world will praise and submit itself to the mind of the king who is able to give with affability, and to protect all who come to him

tr: Who guards the realm and justice strict maintains, That king as god o'er subject people reigns
mn: That king, will be esteemed a God among men, who performs his own duties, and protects (his subjects).

tr: The king of worth, who can words bitter to his ear endure, Beneath the shadow of his power the world abides secure
mn: The whole world will dwell under the umbrella of the king, who can bear words that embitter the ear

tr: Gifts, grace, right sceptre, care of people's weal; These four a light of dreaded kings reveal
mn: He is the light of kings who has there four things, beneficence, benevolence, rectitude, and care for his people

tr: So learn that you may full and faultless learning gain, Then in obedience meet to lessons learnt remain
mn: Let a man learn thoroughly whatever he may learn, and let his conduct be worthy of his learning

tr: The twain that lore of numbers and of letters giveAre eyes, the wise declare, to all on earth that live
mn: Letters and numbers are the two eyes of man

tr: Men who learning gain have eyes, men say; Blockheads' faces pairs of sores display
mn: The learned are said to have eyes, but the unlearned have (merely) two sores in their face

tr: You meet with joy, with pleasant thought you part; Such is the learned scholar's wonderous art
mn: It is the part of the learned to give joy to those whom they meet, and on leaving, to make them think (Oh! when shall we meet them again.)

tr: With soul submiss they stand, as paupers front a rich man's face; Yet learned men are first; th'unlearned stand in lowest place
mn: The unlearned are inferior to the learned, before whom they stand begging, as the destitute before the wealthy

tr: In sandy soil, when deep you delve, you reach the springs below; The more you learn, the freer streams of wisdom flow
mn: Water will flow from a well in the sand in proportion to the depth to which it is dug, and knowledge will flow from a man in proportion to his learning

tr: The learned make each land their own, in every city find a home; Who, till they die; learn nought, along what weary ways they roam
mn: How is it that any one can remain without learning, even to his death, when (to the learned man) every country is his own (country), and every town his own (town) ?

tr: The man who store of learning gains, In one, through seven worlds, bliss attains
mn: The learning, which a man has acquired in one birth, will yield him pleasure during seven births

tr: Their joy is joy of all the world, they see; thus moreThe learners learn to love their cherished lore
mn: The learned will long (for more learning), when they see that while it gives pleasure to themselves, the world also derives pleasure from it

tr: Learning is excellence of wealth that none destroy; To man nought else affords reality of joy
mn: Learning is the true imperishable riches; all other things are not riches

tr: Like those at draughts would play without the chequered square, Men void of ample lore would counsels of the learned share
mn: To speak in an assembly (of the learned) without fullness of knowledge, is like playing at chess (on a board) without squares

tr: Like those who doat on hoyden's undeveloped charms are they, Of learning void, who eagerly their power of words display
mn: The desire of the unlearned to speak (in an assembly), is like a woman without breasts desiring (the enjoyment of ) woman-hood

tr: The blockheads, too, may men of worth appear, If they can keep from speaking where the learned hear
mn: The unlearned also are very excellent men, if they know how to keep silence before the learned

tr: From blockheads' lips, when words of wisdom glibly flow, The wise receive them not, though good they seem to show
mn: Although the natural knowledge of an unlearned man may be very good, the wise will not accept for true knowledge

tr: As worthless shows the worth of man unlearned, When council meets, by words he speaks discerned
mn: The self-conceit of an unlearned man will fade away, as soon as he speaks in an assembly (of

tr: 'They are': so much is true of men untaught; But, like a barren field, they yield us nought
mn: The unlearned are like worthless barren land: all that can be said of them is, that they exist

tr: Who lack the power of subtle, large, and penetrating sense, Like puppet, decked with ornaments of clay, their beauty's vain pretence
mn: The beauty and goodness of one who is destitute of knowledge by the study of great and exquisite works, is like (the beauty and goodness) of a painted earthen doll

tr: To men unlearned, from fortune's favour greater-evil springsThan poverty to men of goodly wisdom brings
mn: Wealth, gained by the unlearned, will give more sorrow than the poverty which may come upon the learned

tr: Lower are men unlearned, though noble be their race, Than low-born men adorned with learning's grace
mn: The unlearned, though born in a high caste, are not equal in dignity to the learned; though they may have been born in a low caste

tr: Learning's irradiating grace who gain, Others excel, as men the bestial train
mn: As beasts by the side of men, so are other men by the side of those who are learned in celebrated works

tr: Wealth of wealth is wealth acquired be ear attent; Wealth mid all wealth supremely excellent
mn: Wealth (gained) by the ear is wealth of wealth; that wealth is the chief of all wealth

tr: When 'tis no longer time the listening ear to feedWith trifling dole of food supply the body's need
mn: When there is no food for the ear, give a little also to the stomach

tr: Who feed their ear with learned teachings rare, Are like the happy gods oblations rich who share
mn: Those who in this world enjoy instruction which is the food of the ear, are equal to the Gods, who enjoy the food of the sacrifices

tr: Though learning none hath he, yet let him hear alway:In weakness this shall prove a staff and stay
mn: Although a man be without learning, let him listen (to the teaching of the learned); that will be to him a staff in adversity

tr: Like staff in hand of him in slippery ground who straysAre words from mouth of those who walk in righteous ways
mn: The words of the good are like a staff in a slippery place

tr: Let each man good things learn, for e'en as heShall learn, he gains increase of perfect dignity
mn: Let a man listen, never so little, to good (instruction), even that will bring him great dignity

tr: Not e'en through inadvertence speak they foolish word, With clear discerning mind who've learning's ample lessons heard
mn: Not even when they have imperfectly understood (a matter), will those men speak foolishly, who have profoundly studied and diligently listened (to instruction)

tr: Where teaching hath not oped the learner's ear, The man may listen, but he scarce can hear
mn: The ear which has not been bored by instruction, although it hears, is deaf

tr: 'Tis hard for mouth to utter gentle, modest word, When ears discourse of lore refined have never heard
mn: It is a rare thing to find modesty, a reverend mouth- with those who have not received choice instruction

tr: His mouth can taste, but ear no taste of joy can give!What matter if he die, or prosperous live
mn: What does it matter whether those men live or die, who can judge of tastes by the mouth, and not by the ear ?

tr: True wisdom wards off woes, A circling fortress high; Its inner strength man's eager foes Unshaken will defy
mn: Wisdom is a weapon to ward off destruction; it is an inner fortress which enemies cannot destroy

tr: Wisdom restrains, nor suffers mind to wander where it would; From every evil calls it back, and guides in way of good
mn: Not to permit the mind to go where it lists, to keep it from evil, and to employ it in good, this is wisdom

tr: Though things diverse from divers sages' lips we learn,'Tis wisdom's part in each the true thing to discern
mn: To discern the truth in every thing, by whomsoever spoken, is wisdom

tr: Wisdom hath use of lucid speech, words that acceptance win, And subtle sense of other men's discourse takes in
mn: To speak so as that the meaning may easily enter the mind of the hearer, and to discern the subtlest thought which may lie hidden in the words of others, this is wisdom

tr: Wisdom embraces frank the world, to no caprice exposed; Unlike the lotus flower, now opened wide, now petals strictly closed
mn: To secure the friendship of the great is true wisdom; it is (also) wisdom to keep (that friendship unchanged, and) not opening and closing (like the lotus flower)

tr: As dwells the world, so with the world to dwellIn harmony- this is to wisely live and well
mn: To live as the world lives, is wisdom

tr: The wise discern, the foolish fail to see, And minds prepare for things about to be
mn: The wise are those who know beforehand what will happen; those who do not know this are the unwise

tr: Folly meets fearful ills with fearless heart; To fear where cause of fear exists is wisdom's part
mn: Not to fear what ought to be feared, is folly; it is the work of the wise to fear what should be feared

tr: The wise with watchful soul who coming ills foresee; From coming evil's dreaded shock are free
mn: No terrifying calamity will happen to the wise, who (foresee) and guard against coming evils

tr: The wise is rich, with ev'ry blessing blest; The fool is poor, of everything possessed
mn: Those who possess wisdom, possess every thing; those who have not wisdom, whatever they may possess, have nothing

tr: Who arrogance, and wrath, and littleness of low desire restrain, To sure increase of lofty dignity attain
mn: Truly great is the excellence of those (kings) who are free from pride, anger, and lust

tr: A niggard hand, o'erweening self-regard, and mirthUnseemly, bring disgrace to men of kingly brith
mn: Avarice, undignified pride, and low pleasures are faults in a king

tr: Though small as millet-seed the fault men deem; As palm tree vast to those who fear disgrace 'twill seem
mn: Those who fear guilt, if they commit a fault small as a millet seed, will consider it to be as large as a palmyra tree

tr: Freedom from faults is wealth; watch heedfully'Gainst these, for fault is fatal enmity
mn: Guard against faults as a matter (of great consequence; for) faults are a deadly enemy

tr: His joy who guards not 'gainst the coming evil day, Like straw before the fire shall swift consume away
mn: The prosperity of him who does not timely guard against faults, will perish like straw before fire

tr: Faultless the king who first his own faults cures, and thenPermits himself to scan faults of other men
mn: What fault will remain in the king who has put away his own evils, and looks after the evils of others

tr: Who leaves undone what should be done, with niggard mind, His wealth shall perish, leaving not a wrack behind
mn: The wealth of the avaricious man, who does not expend it for the purposes for which he ought to expend it will waste away and not continue

tr: The greed of soul that avarice men call, When faults are summed, is worst of all
mn: Griping avarice is not to be reckoned as one among other faults; (it stands alone - greater than all)

tr: Never indulge in self-complaisant mood, Nor deed desire that yields no gain of good
mn: Let no (one) praise himself, at any time; let him not desire to do useless things

tr: If, to your foes unknown, you cherish what you love, Counsels of men who wish you harm will harmless prove
mn: If (a king) enjoys, privately the things which he desires, the designs of his enemies will be useless

tr: As friends the men who virtue know, and riper wisdom share, Their worth weighed well, the king should choose with care
mn: Let (a king) ponder well its value, and secure the friendship of men of virtue and of mature knowledge
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: Cherish the all-accomplished men as friends, Whose skill the present ill removes, from coming ill defends
mn: Let (a king) procure and kindly care for men who can overcome difficulties when they occur, and guard against them before they happen
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: To cherish men of mighty soul, and make them all their own, Of kingly treasures rare, as rarest gift is known
mn: To cherish great men and make them his own, is the most difficult of all difficult things
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: To live with men of greatness that their own excels, As cherished friends, is greatest power that with a monarch dwells
mn: So to act as to make those men, his own, who are greater than himself is of all powers the highest
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: The king, since counsellors are monarch's eyes, Should counsellors select with counsel wise
mn: As a king must use his ministers as eyes (in managing his kingdom), let him well examine their character and qualifications before he engages them
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: The king, who knows to live with worthy men allied, Has nought to fear from any foeman's pride
mn: There will be nothing left for enemies to do, against him who has the power of acting (so as to secure) the fellowship of worthy men
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: What power can work his fall, who faithful ministersEmploys, that thunder out reproaches when he errs
mn: Who are great enough to destroy him who has servants that have power to rebuke him ?
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: The king with none to censure him, bereft of safeguards all, Though none his ruin work, shall surely ruined fall
mn: The king, who is without the guard of men who can rebuke him, will perish, even though there be no one to destroy him
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: Who owns no principal, can have no gain of usury; Who lacks support of friends, knows no stability
mn: There can be no gain to those who have no capital; and in like manner there can be no permanence to
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: Than hate of many foes incurred, works greater woeTen-fold, of worthy men the friendship to forego
mn: It is tenfold more injurious to abandon the friendship of the good, than to incur the hatred of the many
cEn: Seeking the Aid of Great Men

tr: The great of soul will mean association fear; The mean of soul regard mean men as kinsmen dear
mn: (True) greatness fears the society of the base; it is only the low - minded who will regard them as friends

tr: The waters' virtues change with soil through which they flow; As man's companionship so will his wisdom show
mn: As water changes (its nature), from the nature of the soil (in which it flows), so will the character of men resemble that of their associates

tr: Perceptions manifold in men are of the mind alone; The value of the man by his companionship is known
mn: The power of knowing is from the mind; (but) his character is from that of his associates

tr: Man's wisdom seems the offspring of his mind;'Tis outcome of companionship we find
mn: Wisdom appears to rest in the mind, but it really exists to a man in his companions

tr: Both purity of mind, and purity of action clear, Leaning no staff of pure companionship, to man draw near
mn: Chaste company is the staff on which come, these two things, viz, purity of mind and purity of conduct

tr: From true pure-minded men a virtuous race proceeds; To men of pure companionship belong no evil deeds
mn: To the pure-minded there will be a good posterity By those whose associates are pure, no deeds will be done that are not good

tr: Goodness of mind to lives of men increaseth gain; And good companionship doth all of praise obtain
mn: Goodness of mind will give wealth, and good society will bring with it all praise, to men

tr: To perfect men, though minds right good belong, Yet good companionship is confirmation strong
mn: Yet good companionship is confirmation strong

tr: Although to mental goodness joys of other life belong, Yet good companionship is confirmation strong
mn: Future bliss is (the result) of goodness of mind; and even this acquires strength from the society of the good

tr: Than good companionship no surer help we know; Than bad companionship nought causes direr woe
mn: There is no greater help than the company of the good; there is no greater source of sorrow than the company of the wicked

tr: Expenditure, return, and profit of the deedIn time to come; weigh these- than to the act proceed
mn: Let a man reflect on what will be lost, what will be acquired and (from these) what will be his ultimate gain, and (then, let him) act

tr: With chosen friends deliberate; next use the private thought; Then act By those who thus proceed all works with ease are wrought
mn: There is nothing too difficult to (be attained by) those who, before they act, reflect well themselves, and thoroughly consider (the matter) with chosen friends

tr: To risk one's all and lose, aiming at added gain, Is rash affair, from which the wise abstain
mn: Wise men will not, in the hopes of profit, undertake works that will consume their principal

tr: A work of which the issue is not clear, Begin not they reproachful scorn who fear
mn: Those who fear reproach will not commence anything which has not been (thoroughly considered) and made clear to them

tr: With plans not well matured to rise against your foe, Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow
mn: One way to promote the prosperity of an enemy, is (for a king) to set out (to war) without having thoroughly weighed his ability (to cope with its chances)

tr: 'Tis ruin if man do an unbefitting thing; Fit things to leave undone will equal ruin bring
mn: He will perish who does not what is not fit to do; and he also will perish who does not do what it is fit to

tr: Think, and then dare the deed! Who cry,'Deed dared, we'll think,' disgraced shall be
mn: Consider, and then undertake a matter; after having undertaken it, to say "We will consider," is folly

tr: On no right system if man toil and strive, Though many men assist, no work can thrive
mn: The work, which is not done by suitable methods, will fail though many stand to uphold it

tr: Though well the work be done, yet one mistake is made, To habitudes of various men when no regard is paid
mn: There are failures even in acting well, when it is done without knowing the various dispositions of men

tr: Plan and perform no work that others may despise; What misbeseems a king the world will not approve as wise
mn: Let a man reflect, and do things which bring no reproach; the world will not approve, with him, of things which do not become of his position to adopt

tr: The force the strife demands, the force he owns, the force of foes, The force of friends; these should he weigh ere to the war he goes
mn: Let (one) weigh well the strength of the deed (he purposes to do), his own strength, the strength of his enemy, and the strength of the allies (of both), and then let him act

tr: Who know what can be wrought, with knowledge of the means, on this, Their mind firm set, go forth, nought goes with them amiss
mn: There is nothing which may not be accomplished by those who, before they attack (an enemy), make themselves acquainted with their own ability, and with whatever else is (needful) to be known, and

tr: Ill-deeming of their proper powers, have many monarchs striven, And midmost of unequal conflict fallen asunder riven
mn: There are many who, ignorant of their (want of) power (to meet it), have haughtily set out to war, and broken down in the midst of it

tr: Who not agrees with those around, no moderation knows, In self-applause indulging, swift to ruin goes
mn: He will quickly perish who, ignorant of his own resources flatters himself of his greatness, and does

tr: With peacock feathers light, you load the wain; Yet, heaped too high, the axle snaps in twain
mn: The axle tree of a bandy, loaded only with peacocks' feathers will break, if it be greatly overloaded

tr: Who daring climbs, and would himself upraiseBeyond the branch's tip, with life the forfeit pays
mn: There will be an end to the life of him who, having climbed out to the end of a branch, ventures to go further

tr: With knowledge of the measure due, as virtue bids you give!That is the way to guard your wealth, and seemly live
mn: Let a man know the measure of his ability (to give), and let him give accordingly; such giving is the way to preserve his property

tr: Incomings may be scant; but yet, no failure there, If in expenditure you rightly learn to spare
mn: Even though the income (of a king) be small, it will not cause his (ruin), if his outgoings be not larger than his income

tr: Who prosperous lives and of enjoyment knows no bound, His seeming wealth, departing, nowhere shall be found
mn: The prosperity of him who lives without knowing the measure (of his property), will perish, even while it seems to continue

tr: Beneficence that measures not its bound of means, Will swiftly bring to nought the wealth on which it leans
mn: The measure of his wealth will quickly perish, whose liberality weighs not the measure of his property

tr: A crow will conquer owl in broad daylight; The king that foes would crush, needs fitting time to fight
mn: A crow will overcome an owl in the day time; so the king who would conquer his enemy must have (a suitable) time

tr: The bond binds fortune fast is ordered effort made, Strictly observant still of favouring season's aid
mn: Acting at the right season, is a cord that will immoveably bind success (to a king)

tr: Can any work be hard in very fact, If men use fitting means in timely act
mn: Is there anything difficult for him to do, who acts, with (the right) instruments at the right time ?

tr: The pendant world's dominion may be won, In fitting time and place by action done
mn: Though (a man) should meditate (the conquest of) the world, he may accomplish it if he acts in the right time, and at the right place

tr: Who think the pendant world itself to subjugate, With mind unruffled for the fitting time must wait
mn: They who thoughtfully consider and wait for the (right) time (for action), may successfully meditate (the conquest of) the world

tr: The men of mighty power their hidden energies repress, As fighting ram recoils to rush on foe with heavier stress
mn: The self-restraint of the energetic (while waiting for a suitable opportunity), is like the drawing back of a fighting-ram in order to butt

tr: The glorious once of wrath enkindled make no outward show, At once; they bide their time, while hidden fires within them glow
mn: The wise will not immediately and hastily shew out their anger; they will watch their time, and restrain it within

tr: If foes' detested form they see, with patience let them bear; When fateful hour at last they spy,- the head lies there
mn: If one meets his enemy, let him show him all respect, until the time for his destruction is come; when that is come, his head will be easily brought low

tr: When hardest gain of opportunity at last is won, With promptitude let hardest deed be done
mn: If a rare opportunity occurs, while it lasts, let a man do that which is rarely to be accomplished (but for such an opportunity)

tr: As heron stands with folded wing, so wait in waiting hour; As heron snaps its prey, when fortune smiles, put forth your power
mn: At the time when one should use self-control, let him restrain himself like a heron; and, let him like it, strike, when there is a favourable opportunity

tr: Begin no work of war, depise no foe, Till place where you can wholly circumvent you know
mn: Let not (a king) despise (an enemy), nor undertake any thing (against him), until he has obtained (a suitable) place for besieging him

tr: Though skill in war combine with courage tried on battle-field, The added gain of fort doth great advantage yield
mn: Even to those who are men of power and expedients, an attack in connection with a fortification will yield many advantages

tr: E'en weak ones mightily prevail, if place of strong defence, They find, protect themselves, and work their foes offence
mn: Even the powerless will become powerful and conquer, if they select a proper field (of action), and guard themselves, while they make war on their enemies

tr: The foes who thought to triumph, find their thoughts were vain, If hosts advance, seize vantage ground, and thence the fight maintain
mn: If they who draw near (to fight) choose a suitable place to approach (their enemy), the latter, will have to relinquish the thought which they once entertained, of conquering them

tr: The crocodile prevails in its own flow of water wide, If this it leaves, 'tis slain by anything beside
mn: In deep water, a crocodile will conquer (all other animals); but if it leave the water, other animals will conquer it

tr: The lofty car, with mighty wheel, sails not o'er watery main, The boat that skims the sea, runs not on earth's hard plain
mn: Wide chariots, with mighty wheels, will not run on the ocean; neither will ships that the traverse ocean, move on the earth

tr: Save their own fearless might they need no other aid, If in right place they fight, all due provision made
mn: You will need no other aid than fearlessness, if you thoroughly reflect (on what you are to do), and select (a suitable) place for your operations

tr: If lord of army vast the safe retreat assailOf him whose host is small, his mightiest efforts fail
mn: The power of one who has a large army will perish, if he goes into ground where only a small army can act

tr: Though fort be none, and store of wealth they lack,'Tis hard a people's homesteads to attack
mn: It is a hazardous thing to attack men in their own country, although they may neither have power nor a good fortress

tr: The jackal slays, in miry paths of foot-betraying fen, The elephant of fearless eye and tusks transfixing armed men
mn: A fox can kill a fearless, warrior-faced elephant, if it go into mud in which its legs sink down

tr: How treats he virtue, wealth and pleasure? How, when life's at stake, Comports himself? This four-fold test of man will full assurance make
mn: Let (a minister) be chosen, after he has been tried by means of these four things, viz,-his virtue, (love of) money, (love of) sexual pleasure, and tear of (losing) life

tr: Of noble race, of faultless worth, of generous prideThat shrinks from shame or stain; in him may king confide
mn: (The king's) choice should (fall) on him, who is of good family, who is free from faults, and who has the modesty which fears the wounds (of sin)

tr: Though deeply learned, unflecked by fault, 'tis rare to see, When closely scanned, a man from all unwisdom free
mn: When even men, who have studied the most difficult works, and who are free from faults, are (carefully) examined, it is a rare thing to find them without ignorance

tr: Weigh well the good of each, his failings closely scan, As these or those prevail, so estimate the man
mn: Let (a king) consider (a man's) good qualities, as well as his faults, and then judge (of his character) by that which prevails

tr: Of greatness and of meanness too, The deeds of each are touchstone true
mn: A man's deeds are the touchstone of his greatness and littleness

tr: Beware of trusting men who have no kith of kin; No bonds restrain such men, no shame deters from sin
mn: Let (a king) avoid choosing men who have no relations; such men have no attachment, and thereforehave no fear of crime

tr: By fond affection led who trusts in men of unwise soul, Yields all his being up to folly's blind control
mn: Yields all his being up to folly's blind control

tr: Who trusts an untried stranger, brings disgrace, Remediless, on all his race
mn: Sorrow that will not leave even his posterity will come upon him chooses a stranger whose character he has not known

tr: Trust no man whom you have not fully tried, When tested, in his prudence proved confide
mn: Let (a king) choose no one without previous consideration; after he has made his choice, let him unhesitatingly select for each such duties as are appropriate

tr: Trust where you have not tried, doubt of a friend to feel, Once trusted, wounds inflict that nought can heal
mn: To make choice of one who has not been examined, and to entertain doubts respecting one who has been chosen, will produce irremediable sorrow

tr: Who good and evil scanning, ever makes the good his joy; Such man of virtuous mood should king employ
mn: He should be employed (by a king), whose nature leads him to choose the good, after having weighed both the evil and the good in any undertaking

tr: Who swells the revenues, spreads plenty o'er the land, Seeks out what hinders progress, his the workman's hand
mn: Let him do (the king's) work who can enlarge the sources (of revenue), increase wealth and considerately prevent the accidents (which would destroy it)

tr: A loyal love with wisdom, clearness, mind from avarice free; Who hath these four good gifts should ever trusted be
mn: Let the choice (of a king) fall upon him who largely possesses these four things, love, knowledge, a clear mind and freedom from covetousness

tr: Even when tests of every kind are multiplied, Full many a man proves otherwise, by action tried
mn: Even when (a king) has tried them in every possible way, there are many men who change, from the nature of the works (in which they may be employed)

tr: No specious fav'rite should the king's commission bear, But he that knows, and work performs with patient care
mn: (A king's) work can only be accomplished by a man of wisdom and patient endurance; it is not of a nature to be given to one from mere personal attachment

tr: Let king first ask, 'Who shall the deed perform?' and 'What the deed?'Of hour befitting both assured, let every work proceed
mn: Let (a king) act, after having considered the agent (whom he is to employ), the deed (he desires to do), and the time which is suitable to it

tr: 'This man, this work shall thus work out,' let thoughtful king command; Then leave the matter wholly in his servant's hand
mn: After having considered, "this man can accomplish this, by these means", let (the king) leave with him the discharge of that duty

tr: As each man's special aptitude is known, Bid each man make that special work his own
mn: Having considered what work a man is fit for, let (the king) employ him in that work

tr: Fortune deserts the king who ill can bear, Informal friendly ways of men his tolls who share
mn: Prosperity will leave (the king) who doubts the friendship of the man who steadily labours in the discharge of his duties

tr: Let king search out his servants' deeds each day; When these do right, the world goes rightly on its way
mn: Let a king daily examine the conduct of his servants; if they do not act crookedly, the world will not act crookedly

tr: When wealth is fled, old kindness still to show, Is kindly grace that only kinsmen know
mn: Even when (a man's) property is all gone, relatives will act towards him with their accustomed (kindness)

tr: The gift of kin's unfailing love bestowsMuch gain of good, like flower that fadeless blows
mn: If (a man's) relatives remain attached to him with unchanging love, it will be a source of everincreasing wealth

tr: His joy of life who mingles not with kinsmen gathered round, Is lake where streams pour in, with no encircling bound
mn: The wealth of one who does not mingle freely with his relatives, will be like the filling of water in a

tr: The profit gained by wealth's increase, Is living compassed round by relatives in peace
mn: To live surrounded by relatives, is the advantage to be derived from the acquisition of wealth

tr: Who knows the use of pleasant words, and liberal gifts can give, Connections, heaps of them, surrounding him shall live
mn: He will be surrounded by numerous relatives who manifests generosity and affability

tr: Than one who gifts bestows and wrath restrains, Through the wide world none larger following gains
mn: No one, in all the world, will have so many relatives (about him), as he who makes large gift, and does not give way to anger

tr: The crows conceal not, call their friends to come, then eat; Increase of good such worthy ones shall meet
mn: The crows do not conceal (their prey), but will call out for others (to share with them) while they eat it; wealth will be with those who show a similar disposition (towards their relatives)

tr: Where king regards not all alike, but each in his degree,'Neath such discerning rule many dwell happily
mn: Many relatives will live near a king, when they observe that he does not look on all alike, but that he looks on each man according to his merit

tr: Who once were his, and then forsook him, as beforeWill come around, when cause of disagreement is no more
mn: Those who have been friends and have afterwards forsaken him, will return and join themselves (to him), when the cause of disagreement is not to be found in him

tr: Who causeless went away, then to return, for any cause, ask leave; The king should sift their motives well, consider, and receive
mn: When one may have left him, and for some cause has returned to him, let the king fulfil the object (for which he has come back) and thoughtfully receive him again

tr: 'Tis greater ill, it rapture of o'erweening gladness to the soulBring self-forgetfulness than if transcendent wrath control
mn: More evil than excessive anger, is forgetfulness which springs from the intoxication of great joy

tr: Perpetual, poverty is death to wisdom of the wise; When man forgets himself his glory dies
mn: Forgetfulness will destroy fame, even as constant poverty destroys knowledge

tr: 'To self-oblivious men no praise'; this ruleDecisive wisdom sums of every school
mn: Thoughtlessness will never acquire fame; and this tenet is upheld by all treatises in the world

tr: 'To cowards is no fort's defence'; e'en soThe self-oblivious men no blessing know
mn: Just as the coward has no defence (by whatever fortifications ha may be surrounded), so the thoughtless has no good (whatever advantages he may possess)

tr: To him who nought foresees, recks not of anything, The after woe shall sure repentance bring
mn: The thoughtless man, who provides not against the calamities that may happen, will afterwards repent for his fault

tr: Towards all unswerving, ever watchfulness of soul retain, Where this is found there is no greater gain
mn: There is nothing comparable with the possession of unfailing thoughtfulness at all times; and towards all persons

tr: Though things are arduous deemed, there's nought may not be won, When work with mind's unslumbering energy and thought is done
mn: There is nothing too difficult to be accomplished, if a man set about it carefully, with unflinching endeavour

tr: Let things that merit praise thy watchful soul employ; Who these despise attain through sevenfold births no joy
mn: Let (a man) observe and do these things which have been praised (by the wise); if he neglects and fails to perform them, for him there will be no (happiness) throughout the seven births

tr: Think on the men whom scornful mind hath brought to nought, When exultation overwhelms thy wildered thought
mn: Let (a king) think of those who have been ruined by neglect, when his mind is elated with joy

tr: 'Tis easy what thou hast in mind to gain, If what thou hast in mind thy mind retain
mn: It is easy for (one) to obtain whatever he may think of, if he can again think of it

tr: Search out, to no one favour show; with heart that justice lovesConsult, then act; this is the rule that right approves
mn: To examine into (the crimes which may be committed), to show no favour (to any one), to desire to act with impartiality towards all, and to inflict (such punishments) as may be wisely resolved on,

tr: All earth looks up to heav'n whence raindrops fall; All subjects look to king that ruleth all
mn: When there is rain, the living creation thrives; and so when the king rules justly, his subjects thrive

tr: Learning and virtue of the sages spring, From all-controlling sceptre of the king
mn: The sceptre of the king is the firm support of the Vedas of the Brahmin, and of all virtues therein described

tr: Whose heart embraces subjects all, lord over mighty landWho rules, the world his feet embracing stands
mn: The world will constantly embrace the feet of the great king who rules over his subjects with love

tr: Where king, who righteous laws regards, the sceptre wields, There fall the showers, there rich abundance crowns the fields
mn: Rain and plentiful crops will ever dwell together in the country of the king who sways his sceptre with justice

tr: Not lance gives kings the victory, But sceptre swayed with equity
mn: It is not the javelin that gives victory, but the king's sceptre, if it do no injustice

tr: The king all the whole realm of earth protects; And justice guards the king who right respects
mn: The king defends the whole world; and justice, when administered without defect, defends the king

tr: Hard of access, nought searching out, with partial handThe king who rules, shall sink and perish from the land
mn: The king who gives not facile audience (to those who approach him), and who does not examine and pass judgment (on their complaints), will perish in disgrace

tr: Abroad to guard, at home to punish, bringsNo just reproach; 'tis work assigned to kings
mn: In guarding his subjects (against injury from others), and in preserving them himself; to punish crime

tr: By punishment of death the cruel to restrain, Is as when farmer frees from weeds the tender grain
mn: For a king to punish criminals with death, is like pulling up the weeds in the green corn

tr: Than one who plies the murderer's trade, more cruel is the kingWho all injustice works, his subjects harassing
mn: The king who gives himself up to oppression and acts unjustly (towards his subjects) is more cruel than the man who leads the life of a murderer

tr: As 'Give' the robber cries with lance uplift, So kings with sceptred hand implore a gift
mn: The request (for money) of him who holds the sceptre is like the word of a highway robber who stands with a weapon in hand and says "give up your wealth"

tr: Who makes no daily search for wrongs, nor justly rules, that kingDoth day by day his realm to ruin bring
mn: The country of the king who does not daily examine into the wrongs done and distribute justice, will daily fall to ruin

tr: Whose rod from right deflects, who counsel doth refuse, At once his wealth and people utterly shall lose
mn: The king, who, without reflecting (on its evil consequences), perverts justice, will lose at once both his wealth and his subjects

tr: His people's tears of sorrow past endurance, are not theySharp instruments to wear the monarch's wealth away
mn: Will not the tears, shed by a people who cannot endure the oppression which they suffer (from their king), become a saw to waste away his wealth ?

tr: To rulers' rule stability is sceptre right; When this is not, quenched is the rulers' light
mn: Righteous government gives permanence to (the fame of) kings; without that their fame will have no endurance

tr: As lack of rain to thirsty lands beneath, Is lack of grace in kings to all that breathe
mn: As is the world without rain, so live a people whose king is without kindness

tr: To poverty it adds a sharper sting, To live beneath the sway of unjust king
mn: Property gives more sorrow than poverty, to those who live under the sceptre of a king without justice

tr: Where king from right deflecting, makes unrighteous gain, The seasons change, the clouds pour down no rain
mn: If the king acts contrary to justice, rain will become unseasonable, and the heavens will withhold their showers

tr: Where guardian guardeth not, udder of kine grows dry, And Brahmans' sacred lore will all forgotten lie
mn: If the guardian (of the country) neglects to guard it, the produce of the cows will fail, and the men of six duties viz, the Brahmins will forget the vedas

tr: Who punishes, investigation made in due degree, So as to stay advance of crime, a king is he
mn: He is a king who having equitably examined (any injustice which has been brought to his notice), suitably punishes it, so that it may not be again committed

tr: For length of days with still increasing joys on Heav'n who call, Should raise the rod with brow severe, but let it gently fall
mn: Let the king, who desires that his prosperity may long remain, commence his preliminary enquires with strictness, and then punish with mildness

tr: Where subjects dread of cruel wrongs endure, Ruin to unjust king is swift and sure
mn: The cruel-sceptred king, who acts so as to put his subjects in fear, will certainly and quickly come to ruin

tr: 'Ah! cruel is our king', where subjects sadly say, His age shall dwindle, swift his joy of life decay
mn: The king who is spoken of as cruel will quickly perish; his life becoming shortened

tr: Whom subjects scarce may see, of harsh forbidding countenance; His ample wealth shall waste, blasted by demon's glance
mn: The great wealth of him who is difficult of access and possesses a sternness of countenance, is like that which has been obtained by a devil

tr: The tyrant, harsh in speach and hard of eye, His ample joy, swift fading, soon shall die
mn: The abundant wealth of the king whose words are harsh and whose looks are void of kindness, will instantly perish instead of abiding long, with him

tr: Harsh words and punishments severe beyond the right, Are file that wears away the monarch's conquering might
mn: Severe words and excessive punishments will be a file to waste away a king's power for destroying (his enemies)

tr: Who leaves the work to those around, and thinks of it no more; If he in wrathful mood reprove, his prosperous days are o'er
mn: The prosperity of that king will waste away, who without reflecting (on his affairs himself), commits them to his ministers, and (when a failure occurs) gives way to anger, and rages against them

tr: Who builds no fort whence he may foe defy, In time of war shall fear and swiftly die
mn: The king who has not provided himself with a place of defence, will in times of war be seized with fear and quickly perish

tr: Tyrants with fools their counsels share:Earth can no heavier burthen bear
mn: The earth bears up no greater burden than ignorant men whom a cruel sceptre attaches to itself (as the ministers of its evil deeds)

tr: Since true benignity, that grace exceeding great, residesIn kingly souls, world in happy state abides
mn: The world exists through that greatest ornament (of princes), a gracious demeanour

tr: The world goes on its wonted way, since grace benign is there; All other men are burthen for the earth to bear
mn: The prosperity of the world springs from the kindliness, the existence of those who have no (kindliness) is a burden to the earth

tr: Where not accordant with the song, what use of sounding chordsWhat gain of eye that no benignant light affords
mn: Of what avail is a song if it be inconsistent with harmony ? what is the use of eyes which possess no kindliness

tr: The seeming eye of face gives no expressive light, When not with duly meted kindness bright
mn: Beyond appearing to be in the face, what good do they do, those eyes in which is no well-regulated kindness ?

tr: Benignity is eyes' adorning grace; Without it eyes are wounds disfiguring face
mn: Kind looks are the ornaments of the eyes; without these they will be considered (by the wise) to be merely two sores

tr: Whose eyes 'neath brow infixed diffuse no rayOf grace; like tree in earth infixed are they
mn: They resemble the trees of the earth, who although they have eyes, never look kindly (on others)

tr: Eyeless are they whose eyes with no benignant lustre shine; Who've eyes can never lack the light of grace benign
mn: Men without kind looks are men without eyes; those who (really) have eyes are also not devoid of kind looks

tr: Who can benignant smile, yet leave no work undone; By them as very own may all the earth be won
mn: The world is theirs (kings) who are able to show kindness, without injury to their affairs, (administration of justice)

tr: To smile on those that vex, with kindly face, Enduring long, is most excelling grace
mn: Patiently to bear with, and show kindness to those who grieve us, is the most excellent of all dispositions

tr: They drink with smiling grace, though poison interfused they see, Who seek the praise of all-esteemed courtesy
mn: Those who desire (to cultivate that degree of) urbanity which all shall love, even after swallowing the poison served to them by their friends, will be friendly with them

tr: These two: the code renowned and spies, In these let king confide as eyes
mn: Let a king consider as his eyes these two things, a spy and a book (of laws) universally esteemed

tr: Each day, of every subject every deed,'Tis duty of the king to learn with speed
mn: 'Tis duty of the king to learn with speed

tr: By spies who spies, not weighing things they bring, Nothing can victory give to that unwary king
mn: There is no way for a king to obtain conquests, who knows not the advantage of discoveries made by a spy

tr: His officers, his friends, his enemies, All these who watch are trusty spies
mn: He is a spy who watches all men, to wit, those who are in the king's employment, his relatives, and his enemies

tr: Of unsuspected mien and all-unfearing eyes, Who let no secret out, are trusty spies
mn: A spy is one who is able to assume an appearance which may create no suspicion (in the minds of others), who fears no man's face, and who never reveals (his purpose)

tr: As monk or devotee, through every hindrance making way, A spy, whate'er men do, must watchful mind display
mn: He is a spy who, assuming the appearance of an ascetic, goes into (whatever place he wishes), examines into (all, that is needful), and never discovers himself, whatever may be done to him

tr: A spy must search each hidden matter out, And full report must render, free from doubt
mn: A spy is one who is able to discover what is hidden and who retains no doubt concerning what he has known

tr: Spying by spies, the things they tellTo test by other spies is well
mn: Let not a king receive the information which a spy has discovered and made known to him, until he has examined it by another spy

tr: One spy must not another see: contrive it so; And things by three confirmed as truth you know
mn: Let a king employ spies so that one may have no knowledge of the other; and when the information of three agrees together, let him receive it

tr: Reward not trusty spy in others' sight, Or all the mystery will come to light
mn: Let not a king publicly confer on a spy any marks of his favour; if he does, he will divulge his own secret

tr: 'Tis energy gives men o'er that they own a true control; They nothing own who own not energy of soul
mn: Energy makes out the man of property; as for those who are destitute of it, do they (really) possess what they possess ?

tr: The wealth of mind man owns a real worth imparts, Material wealth man owns endures not, utterly departs
mn: The possession of (energy of) mind is true property; the possession of wealth passes away and abides not

tr: 'Lost is our wealth,' they utter not this cry distressed, The men of firm concentred energy of soul possessed
mn: They who are possessed of enduring energy will not trouble themselves, saying, "we have lost our property."

tr: The man of energy of soul inflexible, Good fortune seeks him out and comes a friend to dwell
mn: Wealth will find its own way to the man of unfailing energy

tr: With rising flood the rising lotus flower its stem unwinds; The dignity of men is measured by their minds
mn: The stalks of water-flowers are proportionate to the depth of water; so is men's greatness proportionate to their minds

tr: Whate'er you ponder, let your aim be loftly still, Fate cannot hinder always, thwart you as it will
mn: In all that a king thinks of, let him think of his greatness; and if it should be thrust from him (by fate), it will have the nature of not being thrust from him

tr: The men of lofty mind quail not in ruin's fateful hour, The elephant retains his dignity mind arrows' deadly shower
mn: The strong minded will not faint, even when all is lost; the elephant stands firm, even when wounded by a shower of arrows

tr: The soulless man can never gainTh' ennobling sense of power with men
mn: Those who have no (greatness of) mind, will not acquire the joy of saying in the world, "we have excercised liaberality"

tr: Huge bulk of elephant with pointed tusk all armed, When tiger threatens shrinks away alarmed
mn: Although the elephant has a large body, and a sharp tusk, yet it fears the attack of the tiger

tr: Firmness of soul in man is real excellance; Others are trees, their human form a mere pretence
mn: Energy is mental wealth; those men who are destitute of it are only trees in the form of men

tr: Of household dignity the lustre beaming bright, Flickers and dies when sluggish foulness dims its light
mn: By the darkness, of idleness, the indestructible lamp of family (rank) will be extinguished

tr: Let indolence, the death of effort, die, If you'd uphold your household's dignity
mn: Let those, who desire that their family may be illustrious, put away all idleness from their conduct

tr: Who fosters indolence within his breast, the silly elf!The house from which he springs shall perish ere himself
mn: The (lustre of the) family of the ignorant man, who acts under the influence of destructive laziness will perish, even before he is dead

tr: His family decays, and faults unheeded thrive, Who, sunk in sloth, for noble objects doth not strive
mn: Family (greatness) will be destroyed, and faults will increase, in those men who give way to laziness, and put forth no dignified exertions

tr: Delay, oblivion, sloth, and sleep: these fourAre pleasure-boat to bear the doomed to ruin's shore
mn: Procrastination, forgetfulness, idleness, and sleep, these four things, form the vessel which is desired by those destined to destruction

tr: Though lords of earth unearned possessions gain, The slothful ones no yield of good obtain
mn: It is a rare thing for the idle, even when possessed of the riches of kings who ruled over the whole earth, to derive any great benefit from it

tr: Who hug their sloth, nor noble works attempt, Shall bear reproofs and words of just contempt
mn: Those who through idleness, and do not engage themselves in dignified exertion, will subject

tr: If sloth a dwelling find mid noble family, Bondsmen to them that hate them shall they be
mn: If idleness take up its abode in a king of high birth, it will make him a slave of his enemies

tr: Who changes slothful habits savesHimself from all that household rule depraves
mn: When a man puts away idleness, the reproach which has come upon himself and his family will disappear

tr: The king whose life from sluggishness is rid, Shall rule o'er all by foot of mighty god bestrid
mn: The king who never gives way to idleness will obtain entire possession of (the whole earth) passed over by him who measured (the worlds) with His foot

tr: Say not, 'Tis hard', in weak, desponding hour, For strenuous effort gives prevailing power
mn: Yield not to the feebleness which says, "this is too difficult to be done"; labour will give the greatness (of mind) which is necessary (to do it)

tr: In action be thou, 'ware of act's defeat; The world leaves those who work leave incomplete
mn: Take care not to give up exertion in the midst of a work; the world will abandon those who abandon their unfinished work

tr: In strenuous effort doth resideThe power of helping others: noble pride
mn: The lustre of munificence will dwell only with the dignity of laboriousness or efforts

tr: Beneficent intent in men by whom no strenuous work is wrought, Like battle-axe in sexless being's hand availeth nought
mn: The liberality of him, who does not labour, will fail, like the manliness of a hermaphrodite, who has a sword in its hand

tr: Whose heart delighteth not in pleasure, but in action finds delight, He wipes away his kinsmen's grief and stands the pillar of their might
mn: He who desires not pleasure, but desires labour, will be a pillar to sustain his relations, wiping away their sorrows

tr: Effort brings fortune's sure increase, Its absence brings to nothingness
mn: Labour will produce wealth; idleness will bring poverty

tr: In sluggishness is seen misfortune's lurid form, the wise declare; Where man unslothful toils, she of the lotus flower is there
mn: They say that the black Mudevi (the goddess of adversity) dwells with laziness, and the Latchmi (the goddess of prosperity) dwells with the labour of the industrious

tr: 'Tis no reproach unpropitious fate should ban; But not to do man's work is foul disgrace to man
mn: Adverse fate is no disgrace to any one; to be without exertion and without knowing what should be known, is disgrace

tr: Though fate-divine should make your labour vain; Effort its labour's sure reward will gain
mn: Although it be said that, through fate, it cannot be attained, yet labour, with bodily exertion, will yield its reward

tr: Who strive with undismayed, unfaltering mind, At length shall leave opposing fate behind
mn: They who labour on, without fear and without fainting will see even fate (put) behind their back

tr: Smile, with patient, hopeful heart, in troublous hour; Meet and so vanquish grief; nothing hath equal power
mn: If troubles come, laugh; there is nothing like that, to press upon and drive away sorrow

tr: Though sorrow, like a flood, comes rolling on, When wise men's mind regards it,- it is gone
mn: A flood of troubles will be overcome by the (courageous) thought which the minds of the wise will entertain, even in sorrow

tr: Who griefs confront with meek, ungrieving heart, From them griefs, put to grief, depart
mn: They give sorrow to sorrow, who in sorrow do not suffer sorrow

tr: Like bullock struggle on through each obstructed way; From such an one will troubles, troubled, roll away
mn: Troubles will vanish (i.e., will be troubled) before the man who (struggles against difficulties) as a

tr: When griefs press on, but fail to crush the patient heart, Then griefs defeated, put to grief, depart
mn: The troubles of that man will be troubled (and disappear) who, however thickly they may come upon him, does not abandon (his purpose)

tr: Who boasted not of wealth, nor gave it all their heart, Will not bemoan the loss, when prosperous days depart
mn: Will those men ever cry out in sorrow, "we are destitute" who, (in their prosperity), give not way to (undue desire) to keep their wealth

tr: 'Man's frame is sorrow's target', the noble mind reflects, Nor meets with troubled mind the sorrows it expects
mn: The great will not regard trouble as trouble, knowing that the body is the butt of trouble

tr: He seeks not joy, to sorrow man is born, he knows; Such man will walk unharmed by touch of human woes
mn: That man never experiences sorrow, who does not seek for pleasure, and who considers distress to be natural (to man)

tr: Mid joys he yields not heart to joys' controlMid sorrows, sorrow cannot touch his soul
mn: He does not suffer sorrow, in sorrow who does not look for pleasure in pleasure

tr: Who pain as pleasure takes, he shall acquireThe bliss to which his foes in vain aspire
mn: The elevation, which even his enemies will esteem, will be gained by him, who regards pain as pleasure

tr: A minister is he who grasps, with wisdom large, Means, time, work's mode, and functions rare he must discharge
mn: The minister is one who can make an excellent choice of means, time, manner of execution, and the difficult undertaking (itself)
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: A minister must greatness own of guardian power, determined mind, Learn'd wisdom, manly effort with the former five combined
mn: The minister is one who in addition to the aforesaid five things excels in the possession of firmness,
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: A minister is he whose power can foes divide, Attach more firmly friends, of severed ones can heal the breaches wide
mn: The minister is one who can effect discord (among foes), maintain the good-will of his friends and restore to friendship those who have seceded (from him)
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: A minister has power to see the methods help afford, To ponder long, then utter calm conclusive word
mn: The minister is one who is able to comprehend (the whole nature of an undertaking), execute it in the best manner possible, and offer assuring advice (in time of necessity)
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: The man who virtue knows, has use of wise and pleasant wordsWith plans for every season apt, in counsel aid affords
mn: He is the best helper (of the king) who understanding the duties, of the latter, is by his special learning, able to tender the fullest advice, and at all times conversant with the best method (of
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: When native subtilty combines with sound scholastic lore,'Tis subtilty surpassing all, which nothing stands before
mn: What (contrivances) are there so acute as to resist those who possess natural acuteness in addition to learning ?
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: Though knowing all that books can teach, 'tis truest tactTo follow common sense of men in act
mn: Though you are acquainted with the (theoretical) methods (of performing an act), understand the ways of the world and act accordingly
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: 'Tis duty of the man in place aloud to sayThe very truth, though unwise king may cast his words away
mn: Although the king be utterly ignorant, it is the duty of the minister to give (him) sound advice
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: A minister who by king's side plots evil thingsWorse woes than countless foemen brings
mn: Far better are seventy crores of enemies (for a king) than a minister at his side who intends (his) ruin
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: For gain of end desired just counsel nought availsTo minister, when tact in execution fails
mn: Those ministers who are destitute of (executive) ability will fail to carry out their projects, although they may have contrived aright
cEn: The Office of Minister of state

tr: A tongue that rightly speaks the right is greatest gain, It stands alone midst goodly things that men obtain
mn: The possession of that goodness which is called the goodness of speech is (even to others) better than any other goodness

tr: Since gain and loss in life on speech depend, From careless slip in speech thyself defend
mn: Since (both) wealth and evil result from (their) speech, ministers should most carefully guard themselves against faultiness therein

tr: 'Tis speech that spell-bound holds the listening ear, While those who have not heard desire to hear
mn: The (minister's) speech is that which seeks (to express) elements as bind his friends (to himself) and is so delivered as to make even his enemies desire (his friendship)

tr: Speak words adapted well to various hearers' state; No higher virtue lives, no gain more surely great
mn: Understand the qualities (of your hearers) and (then) make your speech; for superior to it, there is neither virtue nor wealth

tr: Speak out your speech, when once 'tis past disputeThat none can utter speech that shall your speech refute
mn: Deliver your speech, after assuring yourself that no counter speech can defeat your own

tr: Charming each hearer's ear, of others' words to seize the sense, Is method wise of men of spotless excellence
mn: It is the opinion of those who are free from defects in diplomacy that the minister should speak so as to make his hearers desire (to hear more) and grasp the meaning of what he hears himself

tr: Mighty in word, of unforgetful mind, of fearless speech,'Tis hard for hostile power such man to overreach
mn: It is impossible for any one to conquer him by intrique who possesses power of speech, and is neither faulty nor timid

tr: Swiftly the listening world will gather round, When men of mighty speech the weighty theme propound
mn: If there be those who can speak on various subjects in their proper order and in a pleasing manner, the world would readily accept them

tr: Who have not skill ten faultless words to utter plain, Their tongues will itch with thousand words man's ears to pain
mn: They will desire to utter many words, who do not know how to speak a few faultless ones

tr: Like scentless flower in blooming garland boundAre men who can't their lore acquired to other's ears expound
mn: Those who are unable to set forth their acquirements (before others) are like flowers blossoming in a cluster and yet without fragrance

tr: The good external help confers is worldly gain; By action good men every needed gift obtain
mn: The efficacy of support will yield (only) wealth; (but) the efficacy of action will yield all that is desired

tr: From action evermore thyself restrainOf glory and of good that yields no gain
mn: Ministers should at all times avoid acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit (for the future)

tr: Who tell themselves that nobler things shall yet be wonAll deeds that dim the light of glory must they shun
mn: Those who say, "we will become (better)" should avoid the performance of acts that would destroy (their fame)

tr: Though troubles press, no shameful deed they do, Whose eyes the ever-during vision view
mn: Those who have infallible judgement though threatened with peril will not do acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers)

tr: Do nought that soul repenting must deplore, If thou hast sinned, 'tis well if thou dost sin no more
mn: Let a minister never do acts of which he would have to grieve saying, "what is this I have done"; (but) should he do (them), it were good that he grieved not

tr: Though her that bore thee hung'ring thou behold, no deedDo thou, that men of perfect soul have crime decreed
mn: Though a minister may see his mother starve; let him do not act which the wise would (treat with contempt)

tr: Than store of wealth guilt-laden souls obtain, The sorest poverty of perfect soul is richer gain
mn: Far more excellent is the extreme poverty of the wise than wealth obtained by heaping up of sinful

tr: To those who hate reproof and do forbidden thingWhat prospers now, in after days shall anguish bring
mn: The actions of those, who have not desisted from doing deeds forbidden (by the great), will, even if they succeed, cause them sorrow

tr: What's gained through tears with tears shall go; From loss good deeds entail harvests of blessings grow
mn: All that has been obtained with tears (to the victim) will depart with tears (to himself); but what has been by fair means; though with loss at first, will afterwards yield fruit

tr: In pot of clay unburnt he water pours and would retain, Who seeks by wrong the realm in wealth and safety to maintain
mn: (For a minister) to protect (his king) with wealth obtained by foul means is like preserving a vessel of wet clay by filling it with water

tr: What men call 'power in action' know for 'power of mind'Externe to man all other aids you find
mn: Firmness in action is (simply) one's firmness of mind; all other (abilities) are not of this nature

tr: 'Each hindrance shun', 'unyielding onward press, If obstacle be there,'These two define your way, so those that search out truth declare
mn: Not to perform a ruinous act, and not to be discouraged by the ruinous termination of an act, are the two maxims which, the wise say, from the principles of those who have investigated the subject

tr: Man's fitting work is known but by success achieved; In midst the plan revealed brings ruin ne'er to be retrieved
mn: So to perform an act as to publish it (only) at its termination is (true) manliness; for to announce it beforehand, will cause irremediable sorrow

tr: Easy to every man the speech that shows the way; Hard thing to shape one's life by words they say
mn: To say (how an act is to be performed) is (indeed) easy for any one; but far difficult it is to do according to what has been said

tr: The power in act of men renowned and great, With king acceptance finds and fame through all the state
mn: The firmness in action of those who have become great by the excellence (of their counsel) will, by attaining its fulfilment in the person of the king, be esteemed (by all).

tr: Whate'er men think, ev'n as they think, may men obtain, If those who think can steadfastness of will retain
mn: If those who have planned (an undertaking) possess firmness (in executing it) they will obtain what they have desired even as they have desired it

tr: Despise not men of modest bearing; Look not at form, but what men are:For some there live, high functions sharing, Like linch-pin of the mighty car
mn: Let none be despised for (their) size; (for) the world has those who resemble the linch-pin of the big rolling car

tr: What clearly eye discerns as right, with steadfast will, And mind unslumbering, that should man fulfil
mn: An act that has been firmly resolved on must be as firmly carried out without delay

tr: Though toil and trouble face thee, firm resolve hold fast, And do the deeds that pleasure yield at last
mn: Though it should cause increasing sorrow (at the outset), do with firmness the act that yield bliss (in the end)

tr: The world desires not men of every power possessed, Who power in act desire not,- crown of all the rest
mn: The great will not esteem those who esteem not firmness of action, whatever other abilities the latter may possess

tr: The Resolve is counsel's end, If resolutions halt In weak delays, still unfulfilled, 'tis grievous fault
mn: Consultation ends in forming a resolution (to act); (but) delay in the execution of that resolve is an evil

tr: Slumber when sleepy work's in hand beware Thou slumber not when action calls for sleepless care
mn: Sleep over such (actions) as may be slept over; (but) never over such as may not be slept over

tr: When way is clear, prompt let your action be; When not, watch till some open path you see
mn: Whenever it is possible (to overcome your enemy) the act (of fighting) is certainly good; if not, endeavour to employ some more successful method

tr: With work or foe, when you neglect some little thing, If you reflect, like smouldering fire, 'twill ruin bring
mn: When duly considered, the incomplete execution of an undertaking and hostility will grow and destroy one like the (unextinguished) remnant of a fire

tr: Treasure and instrument and time and deed and place of act These five, till every doubt remove, think o'er with care exact
mn: Do an act after a due consideration of the (following) five, viz money, means, time, execution and place

tr: Accomplishment, the hindrances, large profits won By effort these compare,- then let the work be done
mn: An act is to be performed after considering the exertion required, the obstacles to be encountered, and the great profit to be gained (on its completion)

tr: Who would succeed must thus begin first let him ask The thoughts of them who thoroughly know the task
mn: The method of performance for one who has begun an act is to ascertain the mind of him who knows the secret thereof

tr: By one thing done you reach a second work's accomplishment; So furious elephant to snare its fellow brute is sent
mn: To make one undertaking the means of accomplishing another (similar to it) is like making one rutting elephant the means of capturing another

tr: Than kindly acts to friends more urgent thing to do, Is making foes to cling as friends attached to you
mn: One should rather hasten to secure the alliance of the foes (of one's foes) than perform good offices to one's friends

tr: The men of lesser realm, fearing the people's inward dread, Accepting granted terms, to mightier ruler bow the head
mn: Ministers of small states, afraid of their people being frightened, will yield to and acknowledge their superior foes, if the latter offer them a chance of reconciliation

tr: Benevolence high birth, the courtesy kings love:-These qualities the envoy of a king approve
mn: The qualification of an ambassador are affection (for his relations) a fitting birth, and the possession of attributes pleasing to royalty

tr: Love, knowledge, power of chosen words, three things, Should he possess who speaks the words of kings
mn: Love (to his sovereign), knowledge (of his affairs), and a discriminating power of speech (before other sovereigns) are the three sine qua non qualifications of an ambassador

tr: Mighty in lore amongst the learned must he be, Midst jav'lin-bearing kings who speaks the words of victory
mn: To be powerful in politics among those who are learned (in ethics) is the character of him who speaks

tr: Sense, goodly grace, and knowledge exquisiteWho hath these three for envoy's task is fit
mn: He may go on a mission (to foreign rulers) who has combined in him all these three viz, (natural) sense, an attractive bearing and well-tried learning

tr: In terms concise, avoiding wrathful speech, who utters pleasant word, An envoy he who gains advantage for his lord
mn: He is an ambassador who (in the presence of foreign rulers) speaks briefly, avoids harshness, talks so as to make them smile, and thus brings good (to his own sovereign)

tr: An envoy meet is he, well-learned, of fearless eyeWho speaks right home, prepared for each emergency
mn: He is an ambassador who having studied (politics) talks impressively, is not afraid of angry looks, and knows (to employ) the art suited to the time

tr: He is the best who knows what's due, the time considered well, The place selects, then ponders long ere he his errand tell
mn: He is chief (among ambassadors) who understands the proper decorum (before foreign princes), seeks the (proper) occasion, knows the (most suitable) place, and delivers his message after (due)

tr: Integrity, resources, soul determined, truthfulnessWho rightly speaks his message must these marks possess
mn: The qualifications of him who faithfully delivers his (sovereign's) message are purity, the support (of foreign ministers), and boldness, with truthfulness in addition to the (aforesaid) three
