tr: His faltering lips must utter no unworthy thing, Who stands, with steady eye, to speak the mandates of his king
mn: He alone is fit to communicate (his sovereign's) reply, who possesses the firmness not to utter even inadvertently what may reflect discredit (on the latter)

tr: Death to the faithful one his embassy may bring; To envoy gains assured advantage for his king
mn: He is the ambassador who fearlessly seeks his sovereign's good though it should cost him his life (to deliver his message)

tr: Who warm them at the fire draw not too near, nor keep too much aloof; Thus let them act who dwell beneath of warlike kings the palace-roof
mn: Thus let them act who dwell beneath of warlike kings the palace-roof
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: To those who prize not state that kings are wont to prize, The king himself abundant wealth supplies
mn: For ministers not to cover the things desired by their kings will through the kings themselves yield them everlasting wealth
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: Who would walk warily, let him of greater faults beware; To clear suspicions once aroused is an achievement rare
mn: Ministers who would save themselves should avoid (the commission of) serious errors for if the king's suspicion is once roused, no one can remove it
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: All whispered words and interchange of smiles repress, In presence of the men who kingly power possess
mn: While in the presence of the sovereign, ministers should neither whisper to nor smile at others
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: Seek not, ask not, the secret of the king to hear; But if he lets the matter forth, give ear
mn: (When the king is engaged) in secret counsel (with others), ministers should neither over-hear anything whatever nor pry into it with inquisitive questions, but (wait to) listen when it is divulged (by
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: Knowing the signs, waiting for fitting time, with courteous care, Things not displeasing, needful things, declare
mn: Knowing the (king's disposition and seeking the right time, (the minister) should in a pleasing manner suggest things such as are desirable and not disagreeable
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: Speak pleasant things, but never utter idle word; Not though by monarch's ears with pleasure heard
mn: Ministers should (always) give agreeable advice but on no occasion recommend useless actions, though requested (to do so)
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: Say not, 'He's young, my kinsman,' despising thus your king; But reverence the glory kingly state doth bring
mn: Ministers should behave in accordance with the (Divine) light in the person of kings and not despise them saying, "He is our junior (in age) and connected with our family!"
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: 'We've gained his grace, boots nought what graceless acts we do', So deem not sages who the changeless vision view
mn: Those whose judgement is firm will not do what is disagreeable (to the sovereign) saying (within
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: Who think 'We're ancient friends' and do unseemly things; To these familiarity sure ruin brings
mn: The (foolish) claim with which a minister does unbecoming acts because of his (long) familiarity (with the king) will ensure his ruin
cEn: Conduct in the Presence of the King

tr: Who knows the sign, and reads unuttered thought, the gem is he, Of earth round traversed by the changeless sea
mn: The minister who by looking (at the king) understands his mind without being told (of it), will be a perpetual ornament to the world which is surrounded by a never-drying sea

tr: Undoubting, who the minds of men can scan, As deity regard that gifted man
mn: He is to be esteemed a god who is able to ascertain without a doubt what is within (one's mind)

tr: Who by the sign the signs interprets plain, Give any member up his aid to gain
mn: The king should ever give whatever (is asked) of his belongings and secure him who, by the indications (of his own mind) is able to read those of another

tr: Who reads what's shown by signs, though words unspoken be, In form may seem as other men, in function nobler far is he
mn: Those who understand one's thoughts without being informed (thereof) and those who do not, may (indeed) resemble one another bodily; still are they different (mentally)

tr: By sign who knows not sings to comprehend, what gain,'Mid all his members, from his eyes does he obtain
mn: Of what use are the eyes amongst one's members, if they cannot by their own indications dive those of another ?

tr: As forms around in crystal mirrored clear we find, The face will show what's throbbing in the mind
mn: As the mirror reflects what is near so does the face show what is uppermost in the mind

tr: Than speaking countenance hath aught more prescient skill?Rejoice or burn with rage, 'tis the first herald still
mn: Is there anything so full of knowledge as the face ? (No) it precedes the mind, whether (the latter is) pleased or vexed

tr: To see the face is quite enough, in presence brought, When men can look within and know the lurking thought
mn: If the king gets those who by looking into his mind can understand (and remove) what has occurred (to him) it is enough that he stand looking at their face

tr: The eye speaks out the hate or friendly soul of man; To those who know the eye's swift varying moods to scan
mn: If a king gets ministers who can read the movements of the eye, the eyes (of foreign kings) will (themselves) reveal (to him) their hatred or friendship

tr: The men of keen discerning soul no other test apply(When you their secret ask) than man's revealing eye
mn: The measuring-rod of those (ministers) who say "we are acute" will on inquiry be found to be their (own) eyes and nothing else

tr: Men pure in heart, who know of words the varied force, Should to their audience known adapt their well-arranged discourse
mn: Let the pure who know the arrangement of words speak with deliberation after ascertaining (the nature of) the court (then assembled)
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: Good men to whom the arts of eloquence are known, Should seek occasion meet, and say what well they've made their own
mn: Let the good who know the uses of words speak with a clear knowledge after ascertaining the time (suited to the court)
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: Unversed in councils, who essays to speakKnows not the way of suasive words,- and all is weak
mn: Those who undertake to speak without knowing the (nature of the) court are ignorant of the quality of words as well as devoid of the power (of learning)
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: Before the bright ones shine as doth the lightBefore the dull ones be as purest stucco white
mn: Ministers should be lights in the assembly of the enlightned, but assume the pure whiteness of mortar (ignorance) in that of fools
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: Midst all good things the best is modest grace, That speaks not first before the elders' face
mn: The modesty by which one does not rush forward and speak in (an assembly of) superiors is the best among all (one's) good qualities
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: As in the way one tottering falls, is slip beforeThe men whose minds are filled with varied lore
mn: (For a minister) to blunder in the presence of those who have acquired a vast store of learning and know (the value thereof) is like a good man stumbling (and falling away) from the path (of virtue)
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: The learning of the learned sage shines brightTo those whose faultless skill can value it aright
mn: The learning of those who have read and understood (much) will shine in the assembly of those who faultlessly examine (the nature of) words
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: To speak where understanding hearers you obtain, Is sprinkling water on the fields of growing grain
mn: Lecturing to those who have the ability to understand (for themselves) is like watering a bed of plants that are growing (of themselves)
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: In councils of the good, who speak good things with penetrating power, In councils of the mean, let them say nought, e'en in oblivious hour
mn: Those who are able to speak good things impressively in an assembly of the good should not even forgetfully speak them in that of the low
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: Ambrosia in the sewer spilt, is wordSpoken in presence of the alien herd
mn: To utter (a good word) in the assembly of those who are of inferior rank is like dropping nectar on the ground
cEn: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber

tr: Men, pure in heart, who know of words the varied force, The mighty council's moods discern, nor fail in their discourse
mn: The pure who know the classification of words having first ascertained the nature (of the court) will not (through fear) falter in their speech before the powerful body

tr: Who what they've learned, in penetrating words heve learned to say, Before the learn'd among the learn'd most learn'd are they
mn: Those who can agreeably set forth their acquirements before the learned will be regarded as the most learned among the learned

tr: Many encountering death in face of foe will hold their ground; Who speak undaunted in the council hall are rarely found
mn: Many indeed may (fearlessly) die in the presence of (their) foes; (but) few are those who are fearless in the assembly (of the learned)

tr: What you have learned, in penetrating words speak out beforeThe learn'd; but learn what men more learn'd can teach you more
mn: (Ministers) should agreeably set forth their acquirements before the learned and acquire more (knowledge) from their superiors (in learning)

tr: By rule, to dialectic art your mind apply, That in the council fearless you may make an apt reply
mn: In order to reply fearlessly before a foreign court, (ministers) should learn logic according to the rules (of grammar)

tr: To those who lack the hero's eye what can the sword availOr science what, to those before the council keen who quail
mn: What have they to do with a sword who are not valiant, or they with learning who are afraid of an intelligent assembly ?

tr: As shining sword before the foe which 'sexless being' bears, Is science learned by him the council's face who fears
mn: The learning of him who is diffident before an assembly is like the shining sword of an hermaphrodite in the presence of his foes

tr: Though many things they've learned, yet useless are they all, To man who cannot well and strongly speak in council hall
mn: Those who cannot agreeably speak good things before a good assembly are indeed unprofitable persons inspite of all their various acquirements

tr: Who, though they've learned, before the council of the good men quake, Than men unlearn'd a lower place must take
mn: They who, though they have learned and understood, are yet afraid of the assembly of the good, are said to be inferior (even) to the illiterate

tr: Who what they've learned, in penetrating words know not to say, The council fearing, though they live, as dead are they
mn: Those who through fear of the assembly are unable to set forth their learning in an interesting manner, though alive, are yet like the dead

tr: Where spreads fertility unfailing, where resides a band, Of virtuous men, and those of ample wealth, call that a 'land'
mn: A kingdom is that in which (those who carry on) a complete cultivation, virtuous persons, and

tr: That is a 'land' which men desire for wealth's abundant share, Yielding rich increase, where calamities are rare
mn: A kingdom is that which is desire for its immense wealth, and which grows greatly in prosperity, being free from destructive causes

tr: When burthens press, it bears; Yet, With unfailing handTo king due tribute pays: that is the 'land'
mn: A kingdom is that which can bear any burden that may be pressed on it (from adjoining kingdoms) and (yet) pay the full tribute to its sovereign

tr: That is a 'land' whose peaceful annals know, Nor famine fierce, nor wasting plague, nor ravage of the foe
mn: A kingdom is that which continues to be free from excessive starvation, irremediable epidemics, and destructive foes

tr: From factions free, and desolating civil strife, and bandOf lurking murderers that king afflict, that is the 'land'
mn: A kingdom is that which is without various (irregular) associations, destructive internal enemies, and murderous savages who (sometimes) harass the sovereign

tr: Chief of all lands is that, where nought disturbs its peace; Or, if invaders come, still yields its rich increase
mn: The learned say that the best kingdom is that which knows no evil (from its foes), and, if injured (at all), suffers no diminution in its fruitfulness

tr: Waters from rains and springs, a mountain near, and waters thence; These make a land, with fortress' sure defence
mn: The constituents of a kingdom are the two waters (from above and below), well situated hills and an undestructible fort

tr: A country's jewels are these five: unfailing health, Fertility, and joy, a sure defence, and wealth
mn: Freedom from epidemics, wealth, produce, happiness and protection (to subjects); these five, the learned, say, are the ornaments of a kingdom

tr: That is a land that yields increase unsought, That is no land whose gifts with toil are bought
mn: The learned say that those are kingdom whose wealth is not laboured for, and those not, whose wealth is only obtained through labour

tr: Though blest with all these varied gifts' increase, A land gains nought that is not with its king at peace
mn: Although in possession of all the above mentioned excellences, these are indeed of no use to a country, in the absence of harmony between the sovereign and the sujects

tr: A fort is wealth to those who act against their foes; Is wealth to them who, fearing, guard themselves from woes
mn: A fort is an object of importance to those who march (against their foes) as well as to those who through fear (of pursuers) would seek it for shelter

tr: A fort is that which owns fount of waters crystal clear, An open space, a hill, and shade of beauteous forest near
mn: A fort is that which has everlasting water, plains, mountains and cool shady forests

tr: Height, breadth, strength, difficult access:Science declares a fort must these possess
mn: The learned say that a fortress is an enclosure having these four (qualities) viz, height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility

tr: A fort must need but slight defence, yet ample be, Defying all the foeman's energy
mn: A fort is that which has an extensive space within, but only small places to be guarded, and such as can destroy the courage of besieging foes

tr: Impregnable, containing ample stores of food, A fort for those within, must be a warlike station good
mn: A fort is that which cannot be captured, which abounds in suitable provisions, and affords a position of easy defence to its inmates

tr: A fort, with all munitions amply stored, In time of need should good reserves afford
mn: A fort is that which has all (needful) things, and excellent heroes that can help it against destruction (by foes)

tr: A fort should be impregnable to foes who gird it round, Or aim there darts from far, or mine beneath the ground
mn: A fort is that which cannot be captured by blockading, assaulting, or undermining it

tr: Howe'er the circling foe may strive access to win, A fort should give the victory to those who guard within
mn: That is a fort whose inmates are able to overcome without losing their ground, even abler men who have besieged it

tr: At outset of the strife a fort should foes dismay; And greatness gain by deeds in every glorious day
mn: A fort is that which derives excellence from the stratagems made (by its inmates) to defeat their enemies in the battlefield

tr: Howe'er majestic castled walls may rise, To craven souls no fortress strength supplies
mn: Although a fort may possess all (the above-said) excellence, it is, as it were without these, if its inmates possess not the excellence of action

tr: Nothing exists save wealth, that canChange man of nought to worthy man
mn: Besides wealth there is nothing that can change people of no importance into those of (some) importance

tr: Those who have nought all will despise; All raise the wealthy to the skies
mn: All despise the poor; (but) all praise the rich

tr: Wealth, the lamp unfailing, speeds to every land, Dispersing darkness at its lord's command
mn: The imperishable light of wealth goes into regions desired (by its owner) and destroys the darkness (of enmity therein)

tr: Their wealth, who blameless means can use aright, Is source of virtue and of choice delight
mn: The wealth acquired with a knowledge of the proper means and without foul practices will yield virtue and happiness

tr: Wealth gained by loss of love and grace, Let man cast off from his embrace
mn: (Kings) should rather avoid than seek the accumulation of wealth which does not flow in with mercy and love

tr: Wealth that falls to him as heir, wealth from the kingdom's dues,
mn: The spoils of slaughtered foes; these are the royal revenues

tr: 'Tis love that kindliness as offspring bears:And wealth as bounteous nurse the infant rears
mn: The child mercy which is borne by love grows under the care of the rich nurse of wealth

tr: As one to view the strife of elephants who takes his stand, On hill he's climbed, is he who works with money in his hand
mn: An undertaking of one who has wealth in one's hands is like viewing an elephant-fight from a hill-top

tr: Make money! Foeman's insolence o'ergrownTo lop away no keener steel is known
mn: Accumulate wealth; it will destroy the arrogance of (your) foes; there is no weapon sharper than it

tr: Who plenteous store of glorious wealth have gained, By them the other two are easily obtained
mn: To those who have honestly acquired an abundance of riches, the other two, (virtue and pleasure) are things easy (of acquisition)

tr: A conquering host, complete in all its limbs, that fears no wound, Mid treasures of the king is chiefest found
mn: The army which is complete in (its) parts and conquers without fear of wounds is the chief wealth of the king

tr: In adverse hour, to face undaunted might of conquering foe, Is bravery that only veteran host can show
mn: Ancient army can alone have the valour which makes it stand by its king at the time of defeat, fearless of wounds and unmindful of its reduced strength

tr: Though, like the sea, the angry mice send forth their battle cry; What then? The dragon breathes upon them, and they die
mn: What if (a host of) hostile rats roar like the sea ? They will perish at the mere breath of the cobra

tr: That is a host, by no defeats, by no desertions shamed, For old hereditary courage famed
mn: That indeed is an army which has stood firm of old without suffering destruction or deserting (to the enemy)

tr: That is a 'host' that joins its ranks, and mightily withstands, Though death with sudden wrath should fall upon its bands
mn: That indeed is an army which is capable of offering a united resistance, even if Yama advances against it with fury

tr: Valour with honour, sure advance in glory's path, with confidence; To warlike host these four are sure defence
mn: Valour, honour, following in the excellent-footsteps (of its predecessors) and trust-worthiness; these four alone constitute the safeguard of an army

tr: A valiant army bears the onslaught, onward goes, Well taught with marshalled ranks to meet their coming foes
mn: That is an army which knowing the art of warding off an impending struggle, can bear against the dust-van (of a hostile force)

tr: Though not in war offensive or defensive skilled; An army gains applause when well equipped and drilled
mn: Though destitute of courage to fight and strength (to endure), an army may yet gain renown by the splendour of its appearance

tr: Where weakness, clinging fear and povertyAre not, the host will gain the victory
mn: An army can triumph (over its foes) if it is free from diminution; irremediable aversion and poverty

tr: Though men abound, all ready for the war, No army is where no fit leaders are
mn: Though an army may contain a large number of permanent soldiers, it cannot last if it has no generals

tr: Ye foes stand not before my lord for many a oneWho did my lord withstand, now stands in stone
mn: O my foes, stand not before my leader; (for) many are those who did so but afterwards stood (in the shape of) statues

tr: Who aims at elephant, though dart should fail, has greater praiseThan he who woodland hare with winged arrow slays
mn: It is more pleasant to hold the dart that has missed an elephant than that which has hit hare in the forest

tr: Fierceness in hour of strife heroic greatness shows; Its edge is kindness to our suffering foes
mn: The learned say that fierceness (incontest with a foe) is indeed great valour; but to become a benefactor in case of accident (to a foe) is the extreme (limit) of that valour

tr: At elephant he hurls the dart in hand; for weapon pressed, He laughs and plucks the javelin from his wounded breast
mn: The hero who after casting the lance in his hand on an elephant, comes (in search of another) will pluck the one (that sticks) in his body and laugh (exultingly)

tr: To hero fearless must it not defeat appear, If he but wink his eye when foemen hurls his spear
mn: Is it not a defeat to the valiant to wink and destroy their ferocious look when a lance in cast at them (by their foe) ?

tr: The heroes, counting up their days, set down as vainEach day when they no glorious wound sustain
mn: The hero will reckon among wasted days all those on which he had not received severe wounds

tr: Who seek for world-wide fame, regardless of their life, The glorious clasp adorns, sign of heroic strife
mn: The fastening of ankle-ring by those who disire a world-wide renown and not (the safety of) their lives is like adorning (themselves)

tr: Fearless they rush where'er 'the tide of battle rolls'; The king's reproof damps not the ardour of their eager souls
mn: The heroes who are not afraid of losing their life in a contest will not cool their ardour, even if the king prohibits (their fighting)

tr: Who says they err, and visits them scorn, Who die and faithful guard the vow they've sworn
mn: Who would reproach with failure those who seal their oath with their death ?

tr: If monarch's eyes o'erflow with tears for hero slain, Who would not beg such boon of glorious death to gain
mn: If (heroes) can so die as to fill with tears the eyes of their rulers, such a death deserves to be obtained even by begging

tr: What so hard for men to gain as friendship trueWhat so sure defence 'gainst all that foe can do
mn: What so sure defence 'gainst all that foe can do?

tr: Friendship with men fulfilled of good Waxes like the crescent moon; Friendship with men of foolish mood, Like the full orb, waneth soon
mn: The friendship of the wise waxes like the new moon; (but) that of fools wanes like the full moon

tr: Learned scroll the more you ponder, Sweeter grows the mental food; So the heart by use grows fonder, Bound in friendship with the good
mn: Like learning, the friendship of the noble, the more it is cultivated, the more delightful does it become

tr: Nor for laughter only friendship all the pleasant day, But for strokes of sharp reproving, when from right you stray
mn: Friendship is to be practised not for the purpose of laughing but for that of being beforehand in giving one another sharp rebukes in case of transgression

tr: Not association constant, not affection's token bind;'Tis the unison of feeling friends unites of kindred mind
mn: Living together and holding frequent intercourse are not necessary (for friendship); (mutual) understanding can alone create a claim for it

tr: Not the face's smile of welcome shows the friend sincere, But the heart's rejoicing gladness when the friend is near
mn: The love that dwells (merely in the smiles of the face is not friendship; (but) that which dwells deep in the smiles of the heart is true friendship

tr: Friendship from ruin saves, in way of virtue keeps; In troublous time, it weeps with him who weeps
mn: (True) friendship turns aside from evil (ways) makes (him) walk in the (good) way, and, in case of loss if shares his sorrow (with him)

tr: As hand of him whose vesture slips away, Friendship at once the coming grief will stay
mn: (True) friendship hastens to the rescue of the afflicted (as readily) as the hand of one whose garment is loosened (before an assembly)

tr: And where is friendship's royal seat? In stable mind, Where friend in every time of need support may find
mn: Friendship may be said to be on its throne when it possesses the power of supporting one at all times and under all circumstances, (in the practice or virtue and wealth)

tr: Mean is the friendship that men blazon forth,'He's thus to me' and 'such to him my worth'
mn: Though friends may praise one another saying, "He is so intimate with us, and we so much (with him)"; (still) such friendship will appear mean

tr: To make an untried man your friend is ruin sure; For friendship formed unbroken must endure
mn: As those who are of a friendly nature will not forsake (a friend) after once loving (him), there is no evil so great as contracting a friendship without due inquiry

tr: Alliance with the man you have not proved and proved again, In length of days will give you mortal pain
mn: The friendship contracted by him who has not made repeated inquiry will in the end grieve (him) to death

tr: Temper, descent, defects, associations freeFrom blame: know these, then let the man be friend to thee
mn: Make friendship (with one) after ascertaining (his) character, birth, defects and the whole of one's relations

tr: Who, born of noble race, from guilt would shrink with shame, Pay any price so you as friend that man may claim
mn: The friendship of one who belongs to a (good) family and is afraid of (being charged with) guilt, is worth even purchasing

tr: Make them your chosen friend whose words repentance move, With power prescription's path to show, while evil they reprove
mn: You should examine and secure the friendship of those who can speak so as to make you weep over a crime (before its commission) or rebuke you severely (after you have done it) and are able to teach

tr: Ruin itself one blessing lends:'Tis staff that measures out one's friends
mn: Even in ruin there is some good; (for) it is a rod by which one may measure fully (the affection of one's) relations

tr: 'Tis gain to any man, the sages say, Friendship of fools to put away
mn: It is indead a gain for one to renounce the friendship of fools

tr: Think not the thoughts that dwarf the soul; nor takeFor friends the men who friends in time of grief forsake
mn: Do not think of things that discourage your mind, nor contract friendship with those who would forsake you in adversity

tr: Of friends deserting us on ruin's brink,'Tis torture e'en in life's last hour to think
mn: The very thought of the friendship of those who have deserted one at the approach of adversity will burn one's mind at the time of death

tr: Cling to the friendship of the spotless one's; whate'er you payRenounce alliance with the men of evil way
mn: Continue to enjoy the friendship of the pure; (but) renounce even with a gift, the friendship of those who do not agree (with the world)

tr: Familiarity is friendship's silent pact, That puts restraint on no familiar act
mn: Imtimate friendship is that which cannot in the least be injured by (things done through the) right (of longstanding intimacy)

tr: Familiar freedom friendship's very frame supplies; To be its savour sweet is duty of the wise
mn: The constituents of friendship are (things done through) the right of intimacy; to be pleased with such a right is the duty of the wise

tr: When to familiar acts men kind response refuse, What fruit from ancient friendship's use
mn: Of what avail is long-standing friendship, if friends do not admit as their own actions done through the right of intimacy ?

tr: When friends unbidden do familiar acts with loving heart, Friends take the kindly deed in friendly part
mn: If friends, through the right of friendship, do (anything) without being asked, the wise will be pleased with them on account of its desirability

tr: Not folly merely, but familiar carelessness, Esteem it, when your friends cause you distress
mn: If friends should perform what is painful, understand that it is owing not only to ignorance, but also to the strong claims of intimacy

tr: Who stand within the bounds quit not, though loss impends, Association with the old familiar friends
mn: Those who stand within the limits (of true friendship) will not even in adversity give up the intimacy of long-standing friends

tr: True friends, well versed in loving ways, Cease not to love, when friend their love betrays
mn: Those who have (long) stood in the path of affection will not give it up even if their friends cause (them) their ruin

tr: In strength of friendship rare of friend's disgrace who will not hear, The day his friend offends will day of grace to him appear
mn: To those who understand that by which they should not listen to (tales about) the faults of their friends, that is a (profitable) day on which the latter may commit a fault

tr: Friendship of old and faithful friends, Who ne'er forsake, the world commends
mn: They will be loved by the world, who have not forsaken the friendship of those with whom they have kept up an unbroken long-standing intimacy

tr: Ill-wishers even wish them well, who guardFor ancient friends, their wonted kind regard
mn: Even enemies will love those who have never changed in their affection to their long-standingfriends

tr: Though evil men should all-absorbing friendship show, Their love had better die away than grow
mn: The decrease of friendship with those who look as if they would eat you up (through excess of love) while they are really destitute of goodness is far better than its increase

tr: What though you gain or lose friendship of men of alien heart, Who when you thrive are friends, and when you fail depart
mn: Of what avail is it to get or lose the friendship of those who love when there is gain and leave when there is none ?

tr: These are alike: the friends who ponder friendship's gainThose who accept whate'er you give, and all the plundering train
mn: Friendship who calculate the profits (of their friendship), prostitutes who are bent on obtaining their gains, and thieves are (all) of the same character

tr: A steed untrained will leave you in the tug of war; Than friends like that to dwell alone is better far
mn: Solitude is more to be desired than the society of those who resemble the untrained horses which throw down (their riders) in the fields of battle

tr: 'Tis better not to gain than gain the friendship profitlessOf men of little minds, who succour fails when dangers press
mn: It is far better to avoid that to contract the evil friendship of the base who cannot protect (their friends) even when appointed to do so

tr: Better ten million times incur the wise man's hate, Than form with foolish men a friendship intimate
mn: The hatred of the wise is ten-million times more profitable than the excessive intimacy of the fool

tr: From foes ten million fold a greater good you gain, Than friendship yields that's formed with laughers vain
mn: What comes from enemies is a hundred million times more profitable than what comes from the friendship of those who cause only laughter

tr: Those men who make a grievous toil of what they doOn your behalf, their friendship silently eschew
mn: Gradually abandon without revealing (beforehand) the friendship of those who pretend inability to carry out what they (really) could do

tr: E'en in a dream the intercourse is bitternessWith men whose deeds are other than their words profess
mn: The friendship of those whose actions do not agree with their words will distress (one) even in (one's) dreams

tr: In anywise maintain not intercourse with those, Who in the house are friends, in hall are slandering foes
mn: Avoid even the least approach to a contraction of friendship with those who would love you in private but ridicule you in public

tr: Anvil where thou shalt smitten be, when men occasion find, Is friendship's form without consenting mind
mn: The friendship of those who behave like friends without inward affection is a weapon that may be thrown when a favourable opportunity presents itself

tr: Friendship of those who seem our kin, but are not really kindWill change from hour to hour like woman's mind
mn: The friendship of those who seem to be friends while they are not, will change like the love of women

tr: To heartfelt goodness men ignoble hardly may attain, Although abundant stores of goodly lore they gain
mn: Though (one's) enemies may have mastered many good books, it will be impossible for them to become truly loving at heart

tr: 'Tis fitting you should dread dissemblers' guile, Whose hearts are bitter while their faces smile
mn: One should fear the deceitful who smile sweetly with their face but never love with their heart

tr: When minds are not in unison, 'its never; just, In any words men speak to put your trust
mn: In nothing whatever is it proper to rely on the words of those who do not love with their heart

tr: Though many goodly words they speak in friendly tone, The words of foes will speedily be known
mn: Though (one's) foes may utter good things as though they were friends, once will at once understand (their evil, import)

tr: To pliant speech from hostile lips give thou no ear;'Tis pliant bow that show the deadly peril near
mn: Since the bending of the bow bespeaks evil, one should not accept (as good) the humiliating speeches of one's foes

tr: In hands that worship weapon ten hidden lies; Such are the tears that fall from foeman's eyes
mn: A weapon may be hid in the very hands with which (one's) foes adore (him) (and) the tears they shed are of the same nature

tr: 'Tis just, when men make much of you, and then despise, To make them smile, and slap in friendship's guise
mn: It is the duty of kings to affect great love but make it die (inwardly); as regard those foes who shew them great friendship but despise them (in their heart)

tr: When time shall come that foes as friends appear, Then thou, to hide a hostile heart, a smiling face may'st wear
mn: When one's foes begin to affect friendship, one should love them with one's looks, and, cherishing no love in the heart, give up (even the former)

tr: What one thing merits folly's special name.Letting gain go, loss for one's own to claim
mn: Folly is one (of the chief defects); it is that which (makes one) incur loss and forego gain

tr: 'Mid follies chiefest folly is to fix your loveOn deeds which to your station unbefitting prove
mn: The greatest folly is that which leads one to take delight in doing what is forbidden

tr: Ashamed of nothing, searching nothing out, of loveless heart, Nought cherishing, 'tis thus the fool will play his part
mn: Shamelessness indifference (to what must be sought after), harshness, and aversion for everything (that ought to be desired) are the qualities of the fool

tr: The sacred law he reads and learns, to other men expounds,-Himself obeys not; where can greater fool be found
mn: There are no greater fools than he who, though he has read and understood (a great deal) and even taught it to others, does not walk according to his own teaching

tr: The fool will merit hell in one brief life on earth, In which he entering sinks through sevenfold round of birth
mn: A fool can procure in a single birth a hell into which he may enter and suffer through all the seven births

tr: When fool some task attempts with uninstructed pains, It fails; nor that alone, himself he binds with chains
mn: If the fool, who knows not how to act undertakes a work, he will (certainly) fail (But) is it all ? He will even adorn himself with fetters

tr: When fools are blessed with fortune's bounteous store, Their foes feed full, their friends are prey to hunger sore
mn: If a fool happens to get an immense fortune, his neighbours will enjoy it while his relations starve

tr: When folly's hand grasps wealth's increase, 'twill beAs when a mad man raves in drunken glee
mn: A fool happening to possess something is like the intoxication of one who is (already) giddy

tr: Friendship of fools is very pleasant thing, Parting with them will leave behind no sting
mn: The friendship between fools is exceedingly delightful (to each other): for at parting there will be

tr: Like him who seeks his couch with unwashed feet, Is fool whose foot intrudes where wise men meet
mn: The appearance of a fool in an assembly of the learned is like placing (one's) unwashed feet on a bed

tr: Want of knowledge, 'mid all wants the sorest want we deem; Want of other things the world will not as want esteem
mn: The want of wisdom is the greatest of all wants; but that of wealth the world will not regard as such

tr: The gift of foolish man, with willing heart bestowed, is nought, But blessing by receiver's penance bought
mn: (The cause of) a fool cheerfully giving (something) is nothing else but the receiver's merit (in a former birth)

tr: With keener anguish foolish men their own hearts wring, Than aught that even malice of their foes can bring
mn: The suffering that fools inflict upon themselves is hardly possible even to foes

tr: What is stupidity? The arrogance that cries,'Behold, we claim the glory of the wise.'
mn: What is called want of wisdom is the vanity which says, "We are wise"

tr: If men what they have never learned assume to know, Upon their real learning's power a doubt 'twill throw
mn: Fools pretending to know what has not been read (by them) will rouse suspicion even as to what they have thoroughly mastered

tr: Fools are they who their nakedness conceal, And yet their faults unveiled reveal
mn: Even to cover one's nakedness would be folly, if (one's) faults were not covered (by forsaking them)

tr: From out his soul who lets the mystic teachings die, Entails upon himself abiding misery
mn: The fool who neglects precious counsel does, of his own accord, a great injury to himself

tr: Advised, he heeds not; of himself knows nothing wise; This man's whole life is all one plague until he dies
mn: The fool will not perform (his duties) even when advised nor ascertain them himself; such a soul is a

tr: That man is blind to eyes that will not see who knowledge shows;-The blind man still in his blind fashion knows
mn: One who would teach a fool will (simply) betray his folly; and the fool would (still) think himself "wise in his own conceit"

tr: Who what the world affirms as false proclaim, O'er all the earth receive a demon's name
mn: He who denies the existence of what the world believes in will be regarded as a demon on earth

tr: Hostility disunion's plague will bring, That evil quality, to every living thing
mn: The disease which fosters the evil of disunion among all creatures is termed hatred by the wise

tr: Though men disunion plan, and do thee much despite'Tis best no enmity to plan, nor evil deeds requite
mn: Though disagreeable things may be done from (a feeling of) disunion, it is far better that nothing painful be done from (that of) hatred

tr: If enmity, that grievous plague, you shun, Endless undying praises shall be won
mn: To rid one-self of the distressing dtsease of hatred will bestow (on one) a never-decreasing imperishable fame

tr: Joy of joys abundant grows, When malice dies that woe of woes
mn: If hatred which is the greatest misery is destroyed, it will yield the greatest delight

tr: If men from enmity can keep their spirits free, Who over them shall gain the victory
mn: Who indeed would think of conquering those who naturally shrink back from hatred ?

tr: The life of those who cherished enmity hold dear, To grievous fault and utter death is near
mn: Failure and ruin are not far from him who says it is sweet to excel in hatred

tr: The very truth that greatness gives their eyes can never see, Who only know to work men woe, fulfilled of enmity
mn: Who only know to work men woe, fulfilled of enmity

tr: 'Tis gain to turn the soul from enmity; Ruin reigns where this hath mastery
mn: Shrinking back from hatred will yield wealth; indulging in its increase will hasten ruin

tr: Men think not hostile thought in fortune's favouring hour, They cherish enmity when in misfortune's power
mn: At the approach of wealth one will not think of hatred (but) to secure one's ruin, one will look to its increase

tr: From enmity do all afflictive evils flow; But friendliness doth wealth of kindly good bestow
mn: All calamities are caused by hatred; but by the delight (of friendship) is caused the great wealth of good virtues

tr: With stronger than thyself, turn from the strife away; With weaker shun not, rather court the fray
mn: Avoid offering resistance to the strong; (but) never fail to cherish enmity towards the weak

tr: No kinsman's love, no strength of friends has he; How can he bear his foeman's enmity
mn: How can he who is unloving, destitute of powerful aids, and himself without strength overcome the might of his foe ?

tr: A craven thing! knows nought, accords with none, gives nought away; To wrath of any foe he falls an easy prey
mn: In the estimation of foes miserably weak is he, who is timid, ignorant, unsociable and niggardly

tr: His wrath still blazes, every secret told; each dayThis man's in every place to every foe an easy prey
mn: He who neither refrains from anger nor keeps his secrets will at all times and in all places be easily conquered by all

tr: No way of right he scans, no precepts bind, no crimes affright, No grace of good he owns; such man's his foes' delight
mn: (A) pleasing (object) to his foes is he who reads not moral works, does nothing that is enjoined by them cares not for reproach and is not possessed of good qualities

tr: Blind in his rage, his lustful passions rage and swell; If such a man mislikes you, like it well
mn: Highly to be desired is the hatred of him whose anger is blind, and whose lust increases beyond measure

tr: Unseemly are his deeds, yet proffering aid, the man draws nigh:His hate- 'tis cheap at any price- be sure to buy
mn: It is indeed necessary to obtain even by purchase the hatred of him who having begun (a work) does what is not conductive (to its accomplishment)

tr: No gracious gifts he owns, faults many cloud his fame; His foes rejoice, for none with kindred claim
mn: He will become friendless who is without (any good) qualities and whose faults are many; (such a character) is a help to (his) foes

tr: The joy of victory is never far removed from thoseWho've luck to meet with ignorant and timid foes
mn: There will be no end of lofty delights to the victorious, if their foes are (both) ignorant and timid

tr: The task of angry war with men unlearned in virtue's loreWho will not meet, glory shall meet him never more
mn: The light (of fame) will never be gained by him who gains not the trifling reputation of having fought an unlearned (foe)

tr: For Hate, that ill-conditioned thing not e'en in jestLet any evil longing rule your breast
mn: The evil of hatred is not of a nature to be desired by one even in sport

tr: Although you hate incur of those whose ploughs are bows, Make not the men whose ploughs are words your foes
mn: Though you may incur the hatred of warriors whose ploughs are bows, incur not that of ministers whose ploughs are words

tr: Than men of mind diseased, a wretch more utterly forlorn, Is he who stands alone, object of many foeman's scorn
mn: He who being alone, incurs the hatred of many is more infatuated than even mad men

tr: The world secure on his dexterity depends, Whose worthy rule can change his foes to friends
mn: Whose worthy rule can change his foes to friends

tr: Without ally, who fights with twofold enemy o'ermatched, Must render one of these a friend attached
mn: He who is alone and helpless while his foes are two should secure one of them as an agreeable help (to himself)

tr: Whether you trust or not, in time of sore distress, Questions of diff'rence or agreement cease to press
mn: Though (one's foe is) aware or not of one's misfortune one should act so as neither to join nor separate (from him)

tr: To those who know them not, complain not of your woes; Nor to your foeman's eyes infirmities disclose
mn: Relate not your suffering even to friends who are ignorant of it, nor refer to your weakness in the presence of your foes

tr: Know thou the way, then do thy part, thyself defend; Thus shall the pride of those that hate thee have an end
mn: The joy of one's foes will be destroyed if one guards oneself by knowing the way (of acting) and securing assistance

tr: Destroy the thorn, while tender point can work thee no offence; Matured by time, 'twill pierce the hand that plucks it thence
mn: A thorny tree should be felled while young, (for) when it is grown it will destroy the hand of the feller

tr: But breathe upon them, and they surely die, Who fail to tame the pride of angry enemy
mn: Those who do not destroy the pride of those who hate (them) will certainly not exist even to breathe

tr: Water and shade, if they unwholesome prove, will bring you painAnd qualities of friends who treacherous act, will be your bane
mn: Shade and water are not pleasant, (if) they cause disease; so are the qualities of (one's) relations not agreeable, (if) they cause pain

tr: Dread not the foes that as drawn swords appear; Friendship of foes, who seem like kinsmen, fear
mn: Fear not foes (who say they would cut) like a sword; (but) fear the friendship of foes (who seemingly

tr: Of hidden hate beware, and guard thy life; In troublous time 'twill deeper wound than potter's knife
mn: Fear internal enmity and guard yourself; (if not) it will destroy (you) in an evil hour, as surely as the tool which cuts the potter's clay

tr: If secret enmities arise that minds pervert, Then even kin unkind will work thee grievous hurt
mn: The secret enmity of a person whose mind in unreformed will lead to many evils causing disaffection among (one's) relations

tr: Amid one's relatives if hidden hath arise,'Twill hurt inflict in deadly wise
mn: If there appears internal hatred in a (king's) family; it will lead to many a fatal crime

tr: If discord finds a place midst those who dwelt at one before,'Tis ever hard to keep destruction from the door
mn: If hatred arises among (one's) own people, it will be hardly possible (for one) to escape death

tr: As casket with its cover, though in one they live alway, No union to the house where hate concealed hath sway
mn: Never indeed will a family subject to internal hatred unite (really) though it may present an apparent union like that of a casket and its lid

tr: As gold with which the file contends is worn away, So strength of house declines where hate concealed hath sway
mn: A family subject to internal hatred will wear out and lose its strength like iron that has been filed away

tr: Though slight as shred of 'seasame' seed it be, Destruction lurks in hidden enmity
mn: Although internal hatred be as small as the fragment of the sesamum (seed), still does destruction dwell in it

tr: Domestic life with those who don't agree, Is dwelling in a shed with snake for company
mn: Living with those who do not agree (with one) is like dwelling with a cobra (in the same) hut

tr: The chiefest care of those who guard themselves from ill, Is not to slight the powers of those who work their mighty will
mn: Not to disregard the power of those who can carry out (their wishes) is more important than all the watchfulness of those who guard (themselves against evil)

tr: If men will lead their lives reckless of great men's will, Such life, through great men's powers, will bring perpetual ill
mn: To behave without respect for the great (rulers) will make them do (us) irremediable evils

tr: Who ruin covet let them shut their ears, and do despiteTo those who, where they list to ruin have the might
mn: If a person desires ruin, let him not listen to the righteous dictates of law, but commit crimes against those who are able to slay (other sovereigns)

tr: When powerless man 'gainst men of power will evil deeds essay, Tis beck'ning with the hand for Death to seize them for its prey
mn: The weak doing evil to the strong is like beckoning Yama to come (and destroy them)

tr: Who dare the fiery wrath of monarchs dread, Where'er they flee, are numbered with the dead
mn: Those who have incurred the wrath of a cruel and mighty potentate will not prosper wherever they may go

tr: Though in the conflagration caught, he may escape from thence:He 'scapes not who in life to great ones gives offence
mn: Though burnt by a fire (from a forest), one may perhaps live; (but) never will he live who has shown disrespect to the great (devotees)

tr: Though every royal gift, and stores of wealth your life should crown, What are they, if the worthy men of mighty virtue frown
mn: If a king incurs the wrath of the righteous great, what will become of his government with its splendid auxiliaries and (all) its untold wealth ?

tr: If they, whose virtues like a mountain rise, are light esteemed; They die from earth who, with their households, ever-during seemed
mn: If (the) hill-like (devotees) resolve on destruction, those who seemed to be everlasting will be destroyed root and branch from the earth

tr: When blazes forth the wrath of men of lofty fame, Kings even fall from high estate and perish in the flame
mn: Kings even fall from high estate and perish in the flame

tr: Though all-surpassing wealth of aid the boast, If men in glorious virtue great are wrath, they're lost
mn: Though in possession of numerous auxiliaries, they will perish who are-exposed to the wrath of the noble whose penance is boundless

tr: Who give their soul to love of wife acquire not nobler gain; Who give their soul to strenuous deeds such meaner joys disdain
mn: Those who lust after their wives will not attain the excellence of virtue; and it is just this that is not desired by those who are bent on acquiring wealth

tr: Who gives himself to love of wife, careless of noble nameHis wealth will clothe him with o'erwhelming shame
mn: The wealth of him who, regardless (of his manliness), devotes himself to his wife's feminine nature will cause great shame (to ali men) and to himself;

tr: Who to his wife submits, his strange, unmanly moodWill daily bring him shame among the good
mn: The frailty that stoops to a wife will always make (her husband) feel ashamed among the good

tr: No glory crowns e'en manly actions wroughtBy him who dreads his wife, nor gives the other world a thought
mn: The undertaking of one, who fears his wife and is therefore destitute of (bliss), will never be applauded

tr: Who quakes before his wife will ever tremble too, Good deeds to men of good deserts to do
mn: He that fears his wife will always be afraid of doing good deeds (even) to the good

tr: Though, like the demi-gods, in bliss they dwell secure from harm, Those have no dignity who fear the housewife's slender arm
mn: They that fear the bamboo-like shoulders of their wives will be destitute of manliness though they may flourish like the Gods

tr: The dignity of modest womanhood excelsHis manliness, obedient to a woman's law who dwells
mn: Even shame faced womanhood is more to be esteemed than the shameless manhood that performs

tr: Who to the will of her with beauteous brow their lives conform, Aid not their friends in need, nor acts of charity perform
mn: Those who yield to the wishes of their wives will neither relieve the wants of (their) friends nor perform virtuous deeds

tr: No virtuous deed, no seemly wealth, no pleasure, restsWith them who live obedient to their wives' behests
mn: From those who obey the commands of their wives are to be expected neither deeds of virtue, nor those of wealth nor (even) those of pleasure

tr: Where pleasures of the mind, that dwell in realms of thought, abound, Folly, that springs from overweening woman's love, is never found
mn: The foolishness that results from devotion to a wife will never be found in those who possess a reflecting mind and a prosperity (flowing) therefrom

tr: Those that choice armlets wear who seek not thee with love, But seek thy wealth, their pleasant words will ruin prove
mn: The sweet words of elegant braceleted (prostitutes) who desire (a man) not from affection but from avarice, will cause sorrow

tr: Who weigh the gain, and utter virtuous words with vicious heart, Weighing such women's worth, from their society depart
mn: One must ascertain the character of the ill-natured women who after ascertaining the wealth (of a man) speak (as if they were) good natured-ones, and avoid intercourse (with them)

tr: As one in darkened room, some stranger corpse inarms, Is he who seeks delight in mercenary women's charms
mn: The false embraces of wealth-loving women are like (hired men) embracing a strange corpse in a dark room

tr: Their worthless charms, whose only weal is wealth of gain, From touch of these the wise, who seek the wealth of grace, abstain
mn: The wise who seek the wealth of grace will not desire the base favours of those who regard wealth (and not pleasure) as (their) riches

tr: From contact with their worthless charms, whose charms to all are free, The men with sense of good and lofty wisdom blest will flee;
mn: Those whose knowledge is made excellent by their (natural) sense will not covet the trffling delights

tr: From touch of those who worthless charms, with wanton arts, display, The men who would their own true good maintain will turn away
mn: Those who would spread (the fame of) their own goodness will not desire the shoulders of those, who rejoice in their accomplishments and bestow their despicable favours (on all who pay)

tr: Who cherish alien thoughts while folding in their feigned embrace, These none approach save those devoid of virtue's grace
mn: Those who are destitute of a perfectly (reformed) mind will covet the shoulders of those who embrace (them) while their hearts covet other things

tr: As demoness who lures to ruin woman's treacherous loveTo men devoid of wisdom's searching power will prove
mn: The wise say that to such as are destitute of discerning sense the embraces of faithless women are (as ruinous as those of) the celestail female

tr: The wanton's tender arm, with gleaming jewels decked, Is hell, where sink degraded souls of men abject
mn: The delicate shoulders of prostitutes with excellent jewels are a hell into which are plunged the ignorant base

tr: Women of double minds, strong drink, and dice; to these giv'n o'er, Are those on whom the light of Fortune shines no more
mn: Treacherous women, liquor, and gambling are the associates of such as have forsaken by Fortune

tr: Who love the palm's intoxicating juice, each day, No rev'rence they command, their glory fades away
mn: Those who always thirst after drink will neither inspire fear (in others) nor retain the light (of their fame)

tr: Drink not inebriating draught Let him count well the costWho drinks, by drinking, all good men's esteem is lost
mn: Let no liquor be drunk; if it is desired, let it be drunk by those who care not for esteem of the great

tr: The drunkard's joy is sorrow to his mother's eyes; What must it be in presence of the truly wise
mn: Intoxication is painful even in the presence of (one's) mother; what will it not then be in that of the wise ?

tr: Shame, goodly maid, will turn her back for aye on themWho sin the drunkard's grievous sin, that all condemn
mn: The fair maid of modesty will turn her back on those who are guilty of the great and abominable crime of drunkenness

tr: With gift of goods who self-oblivion buys, Is ignorant of all that man should prize
mn: To give money and purchase unconsciousness is the result of one's ignorance of (one's own actions)

tr: Sleepers are as the dead, no otherwise they seem; Who drink intoxicating draughts, they poison quaff, we deem
mn: They that sleep resemble the deed; (likewise) they that drink are no other than poison-eaters

tr: Who turn aside to drink, and droop their heavy eye, Shall be their townsmen's jest, when they the fault espy
mn: Those who always intoxicate themselves by a private (indulgence in) drink; will have their secrets detected and laughed at by their fellow-townsmen

tr: No more in secret drink, and then deny thy hidden fraud; What in thy mind lies hid shall soon be known abroad
mn: Let (the drunkard) give up saying "I have never drunk"; (for) the moment (he drinks) he will simply betray his former attempt to conceal

tr: Like him who, lamp in hand, would seek one sunk beneath the waveIs he who strives to sober drunken man with reasonings grave
mn: Reasoning with a drunkard is like going under water with a torch in search of a drowned man

tr: When one, in sober interval, a drunken man espies, Does he not think, 'Such is my folly in my revelries'
mn: When (a drunkard) who is sober sees one who is not, it looks as if he remembered not the evil effects of his (own) drink

tr: Seek not the gamester's play; though you should win, Your gain is as the baited hook the fish takes in
mn: Though able to win, let not one desire gambling; (for) even what is won is like a fish swallowing the iron in fish-hook

tr: Is there for gamblers, too, that gaining one a hundred lose, some wayThat they may good obtain, and see a prosperous day
mn: That they may good obtain, and see a prosperous day? Is there indeed a means of livelihood that can bestow happiness on gamblers who gain one and lose a hundred?

tr: If prince unceasing speak of nought but play, Treasure and revenue will pass from him away
mn: If the king is incessantly addicted to the rolling dice in the hope of gain, his wealth and the resources thereof will take their departure and fall into other's hands

tr: Gaming brings many woes, and ruins fair renown; Nothing to want brings men so surely down
mn: There is nothing else that brings (us) poverty like gambling which causes many a misery and destroys (one's) reputation

tr: The dice, and gaming-hall, and gamester's art, they eager sought, Thirsting for gain- the men in other days who came to nought
mn: Penniless are those who by reason of their attachment would never forsake gambling, the gamblingplace and the handling (of dice)

tr: Gambling's Misfortune's other name: o'er whom she casts her veil, They suffer grievous want, and sorrows sore bewail
mn: Those who are swallowed by the goddess called "gambling" will never have their hunger satisfied, but suffer the pangs of hell in the next world

tr: Ancestral wealth and noble fame to ruin haste, If men in gambler's halls their precious moments waste
mn: To waste time at the place of gambling will destroy inherited wealth and goodness of character

tr: Gambling wastes wealth, to falsehood bends the soul: it drives awayAll grace, and leaves the man to utter misery a prey
mn: Gambling destroys property, teaches falsehood, puts an end to benevolence, and brings in misery (here and hereafter)

tr: Clothes, wealth, food, praise, and learning, all departFrom him on gambler's gain who sets his heart
mn: The habit of gambling prevents the attainment of these five: clothing, wealth, food, fame and learning

tr: Howe'er he lose, the gambler's heart is ever in the play; E'en so the soul, despite its griefs, would live on earth alway
mn: As the gambler loves (his vice) the more he loses by it, so does the soul love (the body) the more it suffers through it

tr: The learned books count three, with wind as first; of these, As any one prevail, or fail; 'twill cause disease
mn: If (food and work are either) excessive or deficient, the three things enumerated by (medical) writers, flatulence, biliousness, and phlegm, will cause (one) disease

tr: No need of medicine to heal your body's pain, If, what you ate before digested well, you eat again
mn: No medicine is necessary for him who eats after assuring (himself) that what he has (already) eaten has been digested

tr: Who has a body gained may long the gift retain, If, food digested well, in measure due he eat again
mn: If (one's food has been) digested let one eat with moderation; (for) that is the way to prolong the life of an embodied soul

tr: Knowing the food digested well, when hunger prompteth thee, With constant care, the viands choose that well agree
mn: (First) assure yourself that your food has been digested and never fail to eat, when very hungry, whatever is not disagreeable (to you)

tr: With self-denial take the well-selected meal; So shall thy frame no sudden sickness feel
mn: There will be no disaster to one's life if one eats with moderation, food that is not disagreeable

tr: On modest temperance as pleasures pure, So pain attends the greedy epicure
mn: As pleasure dwells with him who eats moderately, so disease (dwells) with the glutton who eats voraciously

tr: Who largely feeds, nor measure of the fire within maintains, That thoughtless man shall feel unmeasured pains
mn: He will be afflicted with numberless diseases, who eats immoderately, ignorant (of the rules of health)

tr: Disease, its cause, what may abate the ill:Let leech examine these, then use his skill
mn: Let the physician enquire into the (nature of the) disease, its cause and its method of cure and treat it faithfully according to (medical rule)

tr: The habitudes of patient and disease, the crises of the illThese must the learned leech think over well, then use his skill
mn: The learned (physician) should ascertain the condition of his patient; the nature of his disease, and the season (of the year) and (then) proceed (with his treatment)

tr: For patient, leech, and remedies, and him who waits by patient's side, The art of medicine must fourfold code of laws provide
mn: Medical science consists of four parts, viz, patient, physician, medicine and compounder; and each of these (again) contains four sub-divisions

tr: Save in the scions of a noble house, you never findInstinctive sense of right and virtuous shame combined
mn: Consistency (of thought, word and deed) and fear (of sin) are conjointly natural only to the high-born

tr: In these three things the men of noble birth fail not:In virtuous deed and truthful word, and chastened thought
mn: The high-born will never deviate from these three; good manners, truthfulness and modesty

tr: The smile, the gift, the pleasant word, unfailing courtesyThese are the signs, they say, of true nobility
mn: A cheerful countenance, liberality, pleasant words, and an unreviling disposition, these four are said to be the proper qualities of the truly high-born

tr: Millions on millions piled would never winThe men of noble race to soul-degrading sin
mn: Though blessed with immense wealth, the noble will never do anything unbecoming

tr: Though stores for charity should fail within, the ancient raceWill never lose its old ancestral grace
mn: Though their means fall off, those born in ancient families, will not lose their character (for liberality)

tr: Whose minds are set to live as fits their sire's unspotted fame, Stooping to low deceit, commit no deeds that gender shame
mn: Those who seek to preserve the irreproachable honour of their families will not viciously do what is detrimental thereto

tr: The faults of men of noble race are seen by every eye, As spots on her bright orb that walks sublime the evening sky
mn: As spots on her bright orb that walks sublime the evening sky

tr: If lack of love appear in those who bear some goodly name,'Twill make men doubt the ancestry they claim
mn: If one of a good family betrays want of affection, his descent from it will be called in question

tr: Of soil the plants that spring thereout will show the worth:The words they speak declare the men of noble birth
mn: As the sprout indicates the nature of the soil, (so) the speech of the noble indicates (that of one's birth)

tr: Who seek for good the grace of virtuous shame must know; Who seek for noble name to all must reverence show
mn: He who desires a good name must desire modesty; and he who desires (the continuance of) a family greatness must be submissive to all

tr: Though linked to splendours man no otherwise may gain, Reject each act that may thine honour's clearness stain
mn: Actions that would degrade (one's) family should not be done; though they may be so important that not doing them would end in death

tr: Who seek with glory to combine honour's untarnished fame, Do no inglorious deeds, though men accord them glory's name
mn: Those who desire (to maintain their) honour, will surely do nothing dishonourable, even for the sake of fame

tr: Bow down thy soul, with increase blest, in happy hour; Lift up thy heart, when stript of all by fortune's power
mn: In great prosperity humility is becoming; dignity, in great adversity

tr: Like hairs from off the head that fall to earth, When fall'n from high estate are men of noble birth
mn: They who have fallen from their (high) position are like the hair which has fallen from the head

tr: If meanness, slight as 'abrus' grain, by men be wrought, Though like a hill their high estate, they sink to nought
mn: Even those who are exalted like a hill will be thought low, if they commit deeds that are debasing

tr: It yields no praise, nor to the land of Gods throws wide the gate:Why follow men who scorn, and at their bidding wait
mn: Why follow men who scorn, and at their bidding wait?

tr: Better 'twere said, 'He's perished!' than to gainThe means to live, following in foeman's train
mn: It is better for a man to be said of him that he died in his usual state than that he eked out his life by following those who disgraced him

tr: When high estate has lost its pride of honour meet, Is life, that nurses this poor flesh, as nectar sweet
mn: For the high-born to keep their body in life when their honour is gone will certainly not prove a remedy against death

tr: Like the wild ox that, of its tuft bereft, will pine away, Are those who, of their honour shorn, will quit the light of day
mn: Those who give up (their) life when (their) honour is at stake are like the yark which kills itself at the loss of (even one of) its hairs

tr: Who, when dishonour comes, refuse to live, their honoured memoryWill live in worship and applause of all the world for aye
mn: The world will (always) praise and adore the fame of the honourable who would rather die than suffer indignity

tr: The light of life is mental energy; disgrace is hisWho says, 'I 'ill lead a happy life devoid of this.'
mn: One's light is the abundance of one's courage; one's darkness is the desire to live destitute of such (a state of mind.)

tr: All men that live are one in circumstances of birth; Diversities of works give each his special worth
mn: All human beings agree as regards their birth but differ as regards their characteristics, because of the different qualities of their actions

tr: The men of lofty line, whose souls are mean, are never greatThe men of lowly birth, when high of soul, are not of low estate
mn: Though (raised) above, the base cannot become great; though (brought) low, the great cannot become base

tr: Like single-hearted women, greatness too, Exists while to itself is true
mn: Exists while to itself is true

tr: The man endowed with greatness true, Rare deeds in perfect wise will do
mn: (Though reduced) the great will be able to perform, in the proper way, deeds difficult (for others to do)

tr: 'As votaries of the truly great we will ourselves enroll,'Is thought that enters not the mind of men of little soul
mn: It is never in the nature of the base to seek the society of the great and partake of their nature

tr: Whene'er distinction lights on some unworthy head, Then deeds of haughty insolence are bred
mn: Even nobility of birth, wealth and learning, if in (the possession of) the base, will (only) produce everincreasing pride

tr: Greatness humbly bends, but littleness alwaysSpreads out its plumes, and loads itself with praise
mn: The great will always humble himself; but the mean will exalt himself in self-admiration

tr: Greatness is absence of conceit; meanness, we deem, Riding on car of vanity supreme
mn: Freedom from conceit is (the nature of true) greatness; (while) obstinacy therein is (that of) meanness

tr: Greatness will hide a neighbour's shame; Meanness his faults to all the world proclaim
mn: The great hide the faults of others; the base only divulge them

tr: All goodly things are duties to the men, they sayWho set themselves to walk in virtue's perfect way
mn: It is said that those who are conscious of their duty and behave with a perfect goodness will regard as natural all that is good

tr: The good of inward excellence they claim, The perfect men; all other good is only good in name
mn: The only delight of the perfect is that of their goodness; all other (sensual) delights are not to be included among any (true) delights

tr: Love, modesty, beneficence, benignant grace, With truth, are pillars five of perfect virtue's resting-place
mn: Affection, fear (of sin), benevolence, favour and truthfulness; these are the five pillars on which perfect goodness rests

tr: The type of 'penitence' is virtuous good that nothing slays; To speak no ill of other men is perfect virtue's praise
mn: Penance consists in the goodness that kills not , and perfection in the goodness that tells not others' faults

tr: Submission is the might of men of mighty acts; the sageWith that same weapon stills his foeman's rage
mn: Stooping (to inferiors) is the strength of those who can accomplish (an undertaking); and that is the weapon with which the great avert their foes

tr: What is perfection's test? The equal mindTo bear repulse from even meaner men resigned
mn: The touch-stone of perfection is to receive a defeat even at the hands of one's inferiors

tr: What fruit doth your perfection yield you, say!Unless to men who work you ill good repay
mn: Of what avail is perfect goodness if it cannot do pleasing things even to those who have pained (it) ?

tr: To soul with perfect virtue's strength endued, Brings no disgrace the lack of every earthly good
mn: Poverty is no disgrace to one who abounds in good qualities

tr: Call them of perfect virtue's sea the shore, Who, though the fates should fail, fail not for evermore
mn: Those who are said to be the shore of the sea of perfection will never change, though ages may change

tr: The mighty earth its burthen to sustain must cease, If perfect virtue of the perfect men decrease
mn: If there is a defect in the character of the perfect, (even) the great world cannot bear (its) burden

tr: Who easy access give to every man, they say, Of kindly courtesy will learn with ease the way
mn: If one is easy of access to all, it will be easy for one to obtain the virtue called goodness

tr: Benevolence and high born dignity, These two are beaten paths of courtesy
mn: Affectionateness and birth in a good family, these two constitute what is called a proper behaviour to all

tr: Men are not one because their members seem alike to outward view; Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true
mn: Resemblance of bodies is no resemblance of souls; true resemblance is the resemblance of qualities that attract

tr: Of men of fruitful life, who kindly benefits dispense, The world unites to praise the 'noble excellence.'
mn: The world applauds the character of those whose usefulness results from their equity and charity

tr: Contempt is evil though in sport They who man's nature know, E'en in their wrath, a courteous mind will show
mn: Reproach is painful to one even in sport; those (therefore) who know the nature of others exhibit (pleasing) qualities even when they are hated

tr: The world abides; for 'worthy' men its weight sustainWere it not so, 'twould fall to dust again
mn: The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good; if not, it would bury itself in the earth and perish

tr: Though sharp their wit as file, as blocks they must remain, Whose souls are void of 'courtesy humane'
mn: He who is destitute of (true) human qualities (only) resembles a tree, though he may possess the sharpness of a file

tr: Though men with all unfriendly acts and wrongs assail,'Tis uttermost disgrace in 'courtesy' to fail
mn: It is wrong (for the wise) not to exhibit (good) qualities even towards those who bearing no friendship (for them) do only what is hateful

tr: To him who knows not how to smile in kindly mirth, Darkness in daytime broods o'er all the vast and mighty earth
mn: To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light

tr: Like sweet milk soured because in filthy vessel poured, Is ample wealth in churlish man's unopened coffers stored
mn: The great wealth obtained by one who has no goodness will perish like pure milk spoilt by the

tr: Who fills his house with ample store, enjoying none, Is dead Nought with the useless heap is done
mn: He who does not enjoy the immense riches he has heaped up in his house, is (to be reckoned as) dead, (for) there is nothing achieved (by him)

tr: Who giving nought, opines from wealth all blessing springs, Degraded birth that doting miser's folly brings
mn: He who knows that wealth yields every pleasure and yet is so blind as to lead miserly life will be born a demon

tr: Who lust to heap up wealth, but glory hold not dear, It burthens earth when on the stage of being they appear
mn: A burden to the earth are men bent on the acquisition of riches and not (true) fame

tr: Whom no one loves, when he shall pass away, What doth he look to leave behind, I pray
mn: What will the miser who is not liked (by any one) regard as his own (in the world to come) ?

tr: Amid accumulated millions they are poor, Who nothing give and nought enjoy of all they store
mn: Those who neither give (to others) nor enjoy (their property) are (truly) destitute, though possessing immense riches

tr: Their ample wealth is misery to men of churlish heart, Who nought themselves enjoy, and nought to worthy men impart
mn: He who enjoys not (his riches) nor relieves the wants of the worthy is a disease to his wealth

tr: Like woman fair in lonelihood who aged grows, Is wealth of him on needy men who nought bestows
mn: The wealth of him who never bestows anything on the destitute is like a woman of beauty growing old without a husband

tr: When he whom no man loves exults in great prosperity,'Tis as when fruits in midmost of the town some poisonous tree
mn: The wealth of him who is disliked (by all) is like the fruit-bearing of the etty tree in the midst of a town

tr: Who love abandon, self-afflict, and virtue's way forsakeTo heap up glittering wealth, their hoards shall others take
mn: To heap up glittering wealth, their hoards shall others take

tr: 'Tis as when rain cloud in the heaven grows day, When generous wealthy man endures brief poverty
mn: The short-lived poverty of those who are noble and rich is like the clouds becoming poor (for a while)

tr: To shrink abashed from evil deed is 'generous shame'; Other is that of bright-browed one of virtuous fame
mn: True modesty is the fear of (evil) deeds; all other modesty is (simply) the bashfulness of virtuous maids

tr: Food, clothing, and other things alike all beings own; By sense of shame the excellence of men is known
mn: Food, clothing and the like are common to all men but modesty is peculiar to the good

tr: All spirits homes of flesh as habitation claim, And perfect virtue ever dwells with shame
mn: As the body is the abode of the spirit, so the excellence of modesty is the abode of perfection

tr: And is not shame an ornament to men of dignity?Without it step of stately pride is piteous thing to see
mn: Is not the modesty ornament of the noble ? Without it, their haughtiness would be a pain (to others)

tr: As home of virtuous shame by all the world the men are known, Who feel ashamed for others, guilt as for their own
mn: The world regards as the abode of modesty him who fear his own and other's guilt

tr: Unless the hedge of shame inviolate remain, For men of lofty soul the earth's vast realms no charms retain
mn: The great make modesty their barrier (of defence) and not the wide world

tr: The men of modest soul for shame would life an offering make, But ne'er abandon virtuous shame for life's dear sake
mn: The modest would rather lose their life for the sake of modesty than lose modesty for the sake of life

tr: Though know'st no shame, while all around asha med must be:Virtue will shrink away ashamed of thee
mn: Virtue is likely to forsake him who shamelessly does what others are ashamed of

tr: 'Twill race consume if right observance fail;'Twill every good consume if shamelessness prevail
mn: Want of manners injures one's family; but want of modesty injures one's character

tr: 'Tis as with strings a wooden puppet apes life's functions, whenThose void of shame within hold intercourse with men
mn: The actions of those who are without modesty at heart are like those of puppet moved by a string

tr: Who says 'I'll do my work, nor slack my hand', His greatness, clothed with dignity supreme, shall stand
mn: There is no higher greatness than that of one saying I will not cease in my effort (to raise my family)
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family

tr: The manly act and knowledge full, when these combineIn deed prolonged, then lengthens out the race's line
mn: One's family is raised by untiring perseverance in both effort and wise contrivances
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family

tr: 'I'll make my race renowned,' if man shall say, With vest succinct the goddess leads the way
mn: The Deity will clothe itself and appear before him who resolves on raising his family
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family

tr: Who labours for his race with unremitting pain, Without a thought spontaneously, his end will gain
mn: Those who are prompt in their efforts (to better their family) need no deliberation, such efforts will of themselves succeed
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family

tr: With blameless life who seeks to build his race's fame, The world shall circle him, and kindred claim
mn: People will eagerly seek the friendship of the prosperous soul who has raised his family without foul means
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family

tr: Of virtuous manliness the world accords the praiseTo him who gives his powers, the house from which he sprang to raise
mn: A man's true manliness consists in making himself the head and benefactor of his family
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family

tr: The fearless hero bears the brunt amid the warrior throng; Amid his kindred so the burthen rests upon the strong
mn: Amid his kindred so the burthen rests upon the strong
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family

tr: Wait for no season, when you would your house uprear;'Twill perish, if you wait supine, or hold your honour dear
mn: As a family suffers by (one's) indolence and false dignity there is to be so season (good or bad) to those who strive to raise their family
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family

tr: Is not his body vase that various sorrows fill, Who would his household screen from every ill
mn: Is it only to suffering that his body is exposed who undertakes to preserve his family from evil ?
cEn: The Way of Maintaining the Family
